status accepted ## context the plasius rendering architecture is moving toward a ray-tracing-first, chunked world pipeline. that architecture depends on a strict separation between authoritative simulation truth and the derived visual state used to prepare a frame. @plasius/gpu-worker already exposes a dag-ready execution plane, but the next wave of renderer and world packages needs a more explicit contract for snapshot-driven scene-preparation work. the preparation pipeline should be able to fan out by chunk, process independent regions in parallel, and join only where stage-local dependencies require it. ## decision @plasius/gpu-worker will treat scene preparation as a first-class dag use case with the following expectations: - scene-preparation jobs consume stable world snapshots rather than mutating in-flight simulation state - manifests may publish multiple roots per chunk or region when unrelated work can start immediately - joins stay local to chunk or representation-stage boundaries rather than forcing global barriers - priority lanes should favor player-near, visible, or otherwise image-critical chunks first - worker manifests should be able to represent the common preparation families: transform propagation, animation, deformation, bounds, lod selection, visibility, light assignment, render-proxy generation, and ray-tracing update preparation ## consequences - positive: renderer and world packages gain one shared execution model for multicore scene preparation. - positive: the worker runtime stays aligned with the lock-free dag scheduler instead of drifting toward package-local orchestration rules. - positive: future packages such as cloth, fluids, or post-processing can describe preparation work through the same snapshot-driven manifest contract. - neutral: package authors still own the semantics of each job family; this adr standardizes orchestration expectations, not package-specific shader logic. ## rejected alternatives - keep scene preparation as an implicit sequence in each consumer package: rejected because that would duplicate scheduling policy and make cross-package budgeting inconsistent. - add a separate scene-preparation scheduler package now: rejected because the existing worker and dag queue packages already cover the execution primitive. ## follow-on work - add a technical decision record for the scene-preparation worker-manifest contract. - add test-first contract and unit specs covering snapshot roots, chunk-local joins, and priority-driven chunk scheduling.

adrs.searchText: gpu-worker plasius-ltd/gpu-worker docs/adrs/adr-0009: drain-until-empty worker invocations.md drain-until-empty worker invocations accepted status context decision consequences rejected alternatives status accepted context @plasius/gpu-worker exists to keep discrete gpu jobs moving through shared queue contracts without each package rebuilding its own scheduling layer. the previous default worker wgsl shape dequeued at most one job per invocation. that was simple, but it leav... decision the published worker wgsl entry point will use drain-until-empty semantics by default. consequences positive: queue-backed workloads can keep workers busy without host-side fences between individual jobs. positive: longer-running or dependency-heavy jobs naturally hold execution resources longer, while shorter jobs let the same invocation pick up more wor... rejected alternatives keep one-job-per-invocation semantics and let callers dispatch more often: rejected because it pushes unnecessary synchronisation and cadence policy back to the host. add package-local drain loops in every consumer package: rejected because @plasius/gpu-wor... the published worker wgsl entry point will use drain-until-empty semantics by default. # adr-0009: drain-until-empty worker invocations ## status accepted ## context @plasius/gpu-worker exists to keep discrete gpu jobs moving through shared queue contracts without each package rebuilding its own scheduling layer. the previous default worker wgsl shape dequeued at most one job per invocation. that was simple, but it leaves throughput on the table for queues that already contain more runnable work. for workloads such as wavefront rendering, fluids, cloth, and lighting refresh, the desired behavior is straightforward: - launch enough invocations to occupy the gpu, - let each invocation dequeue work immediately when it finishes, - avoid host-side waits or per-job synchronisation while runnable work remains. that behavior should be the default in the shared worker runtime, not a package-local workaround. ## decision the published worker wgsl entry point will use drain-until-empty semantics by default. each worker invocation now: 1. attempts to dequeue a job, 2. executes processjob(...), 3. calls completejob(...), 4. immediately loops back to dequeue the next runnable job, 5. exits only when the queue reports no immediately runnable work. the wgsl also exposes an override constant: - workermaxjobsperinvocation: u32 = 0u the default 0u means "no worker-local cap; drain until empty". callers may set a positive pipeline constant when they need to bound per-invocation work for fairness, watchdog, or latency reasons. ## consequences - positive: queue-backed workloads can keep workers busy without host-side fences between individual jobs. - positive: longer-running or dependency-heavy jobs naturally hold execution resources longer, while shorter jobs let the same invocation pick up more work immediately. - positive: dag-ready queues benefit as newly unlocked dependents can be consumed by invocations that are already active. - neutral: packages that need stricter fairness can still opt into a bounded per-invocation job limit through the override constant. ## rejected alternatives - keep one-job-per-invocation semantics and let callers dispatch more often: rejected because it pushes unnecessary synchronisation and cadence policy back to the host. - add package-local drain loops in every consumer package: rejected because @plasius/gpu-worker is the shared execution plane and should own this behavior once.

status: accepted - date: 2026-02-03 ## context we need a deterministic way to generate, store, and render large worlds by splitting them into parts that can be streamed and stitched seamlessly. the system must support multi-lod rendering, keep seams invisible across tiles and lod boundaries, and enable consistent material/shader assignment per terrain type. we also want the pipeline to work with gpu compute prepasses, allow on-demand generation for an effectively infinite world, and emit baked assets that can be reused or distributed. ## decision adopt a tile-based world pipeline with deterministic sampling and explicit lod stitching rules: - partitioning: the world is divided into tiles keyed by (tx, tz, level, tilesizeworld), each with a world size and grid resolution derived from the lod level. tilesizeworld is optional and enables sub-division for complex areas (e.g., cities) without changing the global world rules. - shared borders: each tile generates a (gridsize + 1) vertex lattice so adjacent tiles share identical border samples. a 1–2 cell halo is sampled for normals/filters and discarded after generation. - generation pipeline: gpu compute prepass produces base height + field maps (heat, moisture, rockiness, water). material masks and feature placement are derived from those fields. tiles are generated on demand and can be baked to reusable assets as part of the same pipeline. - lod generation: lower lods are created via deterministic downsampling aligned to parent tiles, then re-classified for materials/features to avoid drift. - stitching: - same-lod seams are avoided by shared border samples. - cross-lod seams use skirts initially, with optional edge-stitch indices and geomorphing for higher fidelity. - shader assignment: tiles store material ids or blend weights; shaders are selected by material classification, not per-tile shader variants. - storage: tile assets cache heightfields, material masks, features, and lod mesh buffers for streaming and reuse. assets are produced from on-demand generation and can be serialized for reuse across sessions or sharing. ## consequences - deterministic sampling enables seamless stitching but requires strict coordinate conventions and halo handling. - lod generation becomes a first-class asset pipeline with extra memory and bake time. - stitching techniques (skirts/edge-stitch/geomorph) must be maintained alongside mesh builders. - tile identity must include tilesizeworld (or equivalent) to avoid mismatched stitching when sub-division is used. - infinite-world streaming requires cache eviction and background bake queues to avoid memory growth. - material assignment is centralized and data-driven, improving consistency but requiring more per-vertex metadata. - supports both offline baking and on-demand generation while keeping the runtime renderer simple.

storage: tile assets cache heightfields, material masks, features, and lod mesh buffers for streaming and reuse. assets are produced from on-demand generation and can be serialized for reuse across sessions or sharing. ## consequences - deterministic sampling enables seamless stitching but requires strict coordinate conventions and halo handling. - lod generation becomes a first-class asset pipeline with extra memory and bake time. - stitching techniques (skirts/edge-stitch/geomorph) must be maintained alongside mesh builders. - tile identity must include tilesizeworld (or equivalent) to avoid mismatched stitching when sub-division is used. - infinite-world streaming requires cache eviction and background bake queues to avoid memory growth. - material assignment is centralized and data-driven, improving consistency but requiring more per-vertex metadata. - supports both offline baking and on-demand generation while keeping the runtime renderer simple.

adrs.title: WebXR Session Management Runtime

headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: Plasius projects need VR session handling that does not depend on Three.js or @react-three/xr. The current website migration target is a zero-Three stack, so XR support must move into a dedicated package that can be consumed by any rendering/runtime layer.

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: Create @plasius/gpu-xr as a framework-agnostic WebXR runtime package.

headingSummaries.heading: Consequences
headingSummaries.summary: Positive: XR handling is reusable across React, vanilla, and worker-driven pipelines. Positive: Three.js can be removed without blocking VR support. Negative: Existing R3F/XR convenience APIs must be replaced at call sites.

headingSummaries.heading: Alternatives Considered
headingSummaries.summary: Continue using @react-three/xr: Rejected because it keeps Three.js coupling. Put XR code inside each app: Rejected due to duplication and drift.

adrs.title: Non-Suspense Hook Contract

headingSummaries.heading: Status
headingSummaries.summary: Accepted Date: 2026-03-06 Version: 1.0

headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: Consumers need predictable loading, error, and revalidation semantics across mixed React runtimes. Suspense can be adopted later, but inconsistent fallback boundaries across hosts would make current behavior hard to reason about.

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: useGraphQuery is explicitly non-suspense in the current contract. Hook state is surfaced via deterministic fields: loading for first fetch without prior data, revalidating for refresh/rerender fetch with prior data, error + status for terminal fetch outcome...

headingSummaries.heading: Consequences
headingSummaries.summary: Consumers have stable behavior without requiring Suspense boundaries. Host apps can migrate to Suspense later via a deliberate ADR and major version update. Hook tests focus on rerender, retry, and revalidation transitions.

adrs.title: Event Ordering Guard and Telemetry Baseline

headingSummaries.heading: Status
headingSummaries.summary: Accepted Date: 2026-03-06 Version: 1.0

headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: Event-driven hydration can corrupt cache state when out-of-order events overwrite newer versions. We also need visibility into event lag and processing failures for operational SLOs.

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: Add version ordering guard before hydration writes; older event versions are skipped. Add schema compatibility guard with configurable supported schema versions. Emit telemetry for: event lag (graph.events.lagms), processed outcomes (graph.events.processed)...

headingSummaries.heading: Consequences
headingSummaries.summary: Out-of-order events no longer overwrite newer cached values. Schema evolution can be rolled out with explicit allow lists. Operational dashboards can track lag/failure while TTL fallback remains the missed-event safety net.

headingSummaries.summary: Accepted Date: 2026-03-06 Version: 1.0

headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: Queue-first degradation requires clear visibility into submit latency, degraded fallback frequency, processing failures, and status-lookup traffic.

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: Add optional telemetry sink to WriteCoordinatorOptions. Emit metrics for submit latency/degradation, processing results, and status lookups. Emit structured errors when partition processing fails.

headingSummaries.heading: Consequences
headingSummaries.summary: Write-path degradation and failure conditions are observable in near real time. Telemetry remains host-configurable with no adapter lock-in.

adrs.title: NFR Analytics and Performance

headingSummaries.heading: Status
headingSummaries.summary: Proposed -> Accepted Date: 2025-09-22 Version: 1.0 Supersedes: N/A Superseded by: N/A

headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: Plasius applications need consistent analytics and performance telemetry with minimal overhead. The solution must be React-friendly, SSR-safe, and allow optional integrations (such as Web Vitals) without forcing heavy dependencies.

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: We will build @plasius/nfr as a focused library for analytics and performance tracking with these structural choices:

headingSummaries.heading: Consequences
headingSummaries.summary: Positive: Consistent telemetry across projects with low overhead and SSR safety. Negative: Requires ongoing maintenance of tracking APIs and compatibility with evolving web APIs. Neutral: Consumers can wire the tracking pipeline to their own backends.

headingSummaries.heading: Alternatives Considered
headingSummaries.summary: Use third-party analytics SDKs directly: Rejected for inconsistent APIs, heavier runtime, and limited SSR control. Per-project tracking utilities: Rejected due to duplication and fragmented behavior.

adrs.title: Enforce OAuth PKCE (S256) Across Backend Login Flows

headingSummaries.heading: Status
headingSummaries.summary: Proposed -> Accepted Date: 2026-02-27 Version: 1.0

headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: Backend OAuth login routes (/oauth/google, /oauth/apple, /oauth/microsoft) previously relied on CSRF state validation without enforced PKCE verifier/challenge binding. Browser-facing code flow security guidance requires PKCE to reduce authorization-code int...

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: Adopt RFC 7636 PKCE with S256 for all backend OAuth authorization starts and callbacks:

headingSummaries.heading: Alternatives Considered
headingSummaries.summary: Keep state-only CSRF protection. Move PKCE generation to frontend callers only.

headingSummaries.heading: Consequences
headingSummaries.summary: Positive: stronger OAuth security baseline and consistent behavior across all login entry points. Negative: additional cookie/state management logic and rollout compatibility handling.

headingSummaries.summary: Adopt a GPU-driven (with small CPU involvement) multi-pass scheduling model using per-task budgets and indirect dispatch/draws. Jobs are grouped by task class, and per-frame budgets cap the number of workgroups/draws per task. This preserves quality-of-serv...

status: accepted - date: 2026-01-23 ## context we need to combine rendering, physics/fluids, particles, ray tracing, and animation while dynamically adjusting quality per frame to keep frame time stable. the system must allow per-frame ratio changes across task types based on scene conditions (e.g., more ray tracing in mirror-heavy areas, fewer particles in water-heavy areas). overhead for this flexibility must stay under 1-5% of total gpu time. a direct "job queue" that dynamically switches vertex/fragment shaders inside a single draw is not possible: pipeline selection happens at command encoding time, not inside a shader. therefore, render workloads must be driven via indirect draws, and compute workloads must be scheduled via compute dispatches. ## decision adopt a gpu-driven (with small cpu involvement) multi-pass scheduling model using per-task budgets and indirect dispatch/draws. jobs are grouped by task class, and per-frame budgets cap the number of workgroups/draws per task. this preserves quality-of-service while keeping overhead low. ### high-level scheduling flow 1. cpu gathers frame stats and sets per-task budgets (workgroups or jobs). 2. gpu budget/dispatch pass computes indirect counts per task. 3. gpu runs compute tasks using dispatchworkgroupsindirect. 4. gpu builds render lists and indirect draw buffers. 5. gpu executes render passes (g-buffer/forward, lighting, transparents). 6. gpu runs ray tracing and denoise passes (budgeted). 7. gpu runs post-processing (taa, tone-map, upscaling). ### task classes (examples) simulation / compute - broadphase collision (sphere/aabb/spatial hash) - inputs: transforms, velocities, bounding volumes, spatial grid/bvh - outputs: potential pair list - narrowphase collision - inputs: pair list, shapes, transforms, velocities - outputs: contact manifolds - solve / integrate - inputs: contacts, forces, constraints - outputs: updated transforms/velocities - fluids (water) - inputs: grid/particles, boundaries, timestep - outputs: updated fluid state, surface/density field - particles (simulation) - inputs: emitters, forces, collision field - outputs: positions/velocities, alive list - animation: muscles + skinning - inputs: skeleton pose, muscle parameters, mesh weights - outputs: skinned positions or skin matrices visibility / scene prep - culling - inputs: transforms, bounds, camera - outputs: visible lists - lod selection - inputs: camera, bounds, lod data - outputs: per-object lod choice - sort/group - inputs: visible list - outputs: pipeline/material-bucketed lists ray tracing - bvh build/refit - inputs: geometry, instances - outputs: tlas/blas - ray tracing - inputs: g-buffer, tlas/blas, lights - outputs: lighting buffers - denoise - inputs: rt buffers, motion vectors - outputs: stabilized lighting rendering - depth pre-pass (optional) - g-buffer or forward pass - lighting resolve (if deferred) - transparent/particle rendering post - taa / motion blur / upscaling - tone mapping / color grading / ui overlay ## options considered 1. single mixed job queue with a big switch in one shader - rejected: diverging control flow and inability to dynamically switch render pipelines. 2. single queue + scatter pass to per-task worklists - acceptable, but adds a pass and extra memory traffic. 3. per-task queues with direct budgeting (chosen) - lowest overhead, simple scheduling, and better cache behavior. ## consequences - requires per-task queues or per-task worklists with indirect dispatch/draw counts. - render tasks are driven by compute-built indirect buffers, not by jobs executing in vertex/fragment directly. - the scheduling pass is o(numtasks) and should stay within the 1-5% overhead budget. - enables dynamic quality control via per-task budgets and per-task quality knobs (iterations, samples, resolution scale). ## implementation notes - budgets can be expressed in workgroups or job counts. - for variable workloads (ray tracing/fluids), pair budgets with quality knobs. - use indirect dispatch and indirect draws to keep cpu involvement minimal and gpu scheduling stable.

headingSummaries.heading: Context

adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site backend/docs/adrs/adr-0006-mcp-admin-safety-and-history.md enforce discovery-first safety rules for mcp admin operations accepted 2026-04-09 context decision consequences context the mcp admin surface is intended for operational tooling, so it must satisfy the backend nfr posture for authorization, rollout control, bounded failures, and auditability. feature 140 also requires explicit rules for destructive confirmation, mutation sco... decision the mcp admin discovery surface adopts the following safety rules: consequences positive: the mcp admin discovery surface adopts the following safety rules: # adr-0006: enforce discovery-first safety rules for mcp admin operations - status: accepted - date: 2026-04-09 ## context the mcp admin surface is intended for operational tooling, so it must satisfy the backend nfr posture for authorization, rollout control, bounded failures, and auditability. feature 140 also requires explicit rules for destructive confirmation, mutation scope, and history retrieval before later mcp features start wiring live mutations. ## decision the mcp admin discovery surface adopts the following safety rules: 1. discovery requires a full authenticated admin session and uses concealed admin authorization. 2. discovery is gated by mcp.admin.foundation.enabled, with mcpadminfoundationenabled reserved as a break-glass override. 3. if the foundation gate is disabled, missing, invalid, or unavailable, the authenticated discovery endpoints return a bounded 503 response with code mcpadminfoundationdisabled. 4. agents must discover a target resource before attempting mutation; no batch mutation or generic backend patch passthrough is permitted in mcp v1. 5. mutation descriptors remain single-resource operations only. 6. destructive operations continue to use /api/ops/destructive-confirmations; mcp does not introduce a second confirmation model. 7. verification and history retrieval reuse /api/ops/audit/events filters instead of adding per-domain history stores. the rollout rollback path is: - disable mcp.admin.foundation.enabled, or - set mcpadminfoundationenabled=false as the emergency local override the evidence required for later mcp mutation features is: - contract tests for discovery output - documentation kept in sync with the registry - audit-verification notes for mutating tools - production-readiness follow-on work under the dedicated mcp hardening feature ## consequences positive: - authenticated admins receive an explicit bounded rollout-disabled response instead of a misleading placeholder contract. - rollback is remote, fast, and does not require redeploying code. - audit-backed verification stays centralized on the existing admin audit store. trade-offs: - discovery remains unavailable until operators enable the foundation rollout gate. - later mcp execution features must preserve the same safety model and cannot bypass destructive confirmation or audit verification for speed. - clients consuming mcp discovery must handle the bounded disabled response during rollout and rollback windows.

adrs.title: Extract Renderer Physics Integration to @plasius/gpu-physics

headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: @plasius/renderer still imported @react-three/rapier directly for scene physics wrappers. That coupling blocks migration sequencing because renderer call sites stay tied to a legacy integration package.

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: Introduce @plasius/gpu-physics as the renderer-facing physics package and migrate renderer call sites to consume its exports.

headingSummaries.heading: Consequences
headingSummaries.summary: Positive: Renderer source no longer imports @react-three/rapier directly. Positive: Future physics backend swaps are localized to one package. Negative: @react-three/rapier is still used transitively until a native replacement lands in @plasius/gpu-physics.

headingSummaries.heading: Alternatives Considered
headingSummaries.summary: Keep direct @react-three/rapier imports in renderer: Rejected because it prevents dependency-boundary migration. Replace full physics backend immediately: Rejected due scope and regression risk for this increment.

adrs.title: Decouple Auth/Profile Consumption from Monorepo Workspace Builds

headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: plasius-ltd-site consumed @plasius/profile while still linking the local packages/profile workspace. Frontend and dashboard TypeScript references and container build steps also depended on that workspace.

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: Decouple profile consumption from local workspace build wiring:

headingSummaries.heading: Consequences
headingSummaries.summary: Positive: Site apps no longer require local profile workspace source builds. Positive: Integration behavior better matches published package usage. Negative: Local source edits in packages/profile no longer auto-propagate through workspace linking.

headingSummaries.heading: Alternatives Considered
headingSummaries.summary: Keep workspace linking for profile: Rejected because it masks package integration issues. Replace all package references with local file links: Rejected because that still violates autonomous package consumption goals.

adrs.title: Enforce OAuth PKCE (S256) for All Login Attempts

headingSummaries.heading: Status
headingSummaries.summary: Accepted Date: 2026-02-27 Version: 1.0

headingSummaries.heading: Tags
headingSummaries.summary: security, oauth, authentication, backend

headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: The backend supports browser-based OAuth login across Google, Apple, and Microsoft. Prior flows used CSRF state checks but did not enforce PKCE end-to-end. Current OAuth guidance (RFC 7636 and OAuth 2.0 Security BCP) expects Authorization Code + PKCE for br...

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: Adopt PKCE (S256) as a required baseline for all backend OAuth authorize redirects and callback token exchanges:

headingSummaries.heading: Alternatives Considered
headingSummaries.summary: Keep state-only CSRF protection: rejected for insufficient protection against authorization-code interception. Generate PKCE only in frontend code: rejected because verifier lifecycle becomes harder to protect and not all login callers use the same frontend...

headingSummaries.heading: Consequences
headingSummaries.summary: Positive: stronger OAuth code-flow security posture, consistent protection across all login entry points, better standards alignment for audits and external review. Negative: additional cookie/state coordination in OAuth routes, temporary compatibility bran...

headingSummaries.heading: References
headingSummaries.summary: RFC 7636 (PKCE): https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7636 RFC 9700 / BCP 240 (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP): https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9700

accepted - date: 2026-02-27 - version: 1.0 ## tags security, oauth, authentication, backend ## context the backend supports browser-based oauth login across google, apple, and microsoft. prior flows used csrf state checks but did not enforce pkce end-to-end. current oauth guidance (rfc 7636 and oauth 2.0 security bcp) expects authorization code + pkce for browser-facing flows. ## decision adopt pkce (s256) as a required baseline for all backend oauth authorize redirects and callback token exchanges: - adrs.title: Backend HTTPS Transport Security Baseline

headingSummaries.heading: Status
headingSummaries.summary: Accepted Date: 2026-02-28 Version: 1.0

headingSummaries.heading: Tags
headingSummaries.summary: security, backend, transport, tls

headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: OAuth PKCE protects authorization code exchange integrity but does not by itself guarantee secure transport for all authenticated API traffic. User confidence requires a consistent backend policy that rejects insecure transport in production and applies har...

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: Adopt a backend transport-security baseline:

headingSummaries.heading: Alternatives Considered
headingSummaries.summary: TLS enforcement only at the edge proxy layer. Route-level opt-in security enforcement.

headingSummaries.heading: Consequences
headingSummaries.summary: Positive: improved anti-MITM posture for user traffic, less chance of insecure route drift, clear operational control via environment configuration. Negative: deployments must correctly pass forwarding headers to avoid false positives.

headingSummaries.heading: References

accepted - date: 2026-02-28 - version: 1.0 ## tags security, devops, deployment, github-actions, azure ## context production deployments were split between a wrapper workflow (cd.yml) and a reusable deployment workflow. this added indirection during incident response and secret-verification troubleshooting. separately, backend runtime credentials were passed as plain environment values during deploy updates. the target model is to source secrets from github production environment secrets and synchronize them into azure container apps secret storage during cd. profile and linked-account work now adds a second requirement: the deployment path must provision a site key vault and expose it to the backend so user-held delegated credentials can be stored only on the server side. ## decision adopt a single deployment workflow, secret-sync model, and key vault bootstrap path: - use only .github/workflows/cd.yml for production deployment orchestration - remove the separate reusable aca deployment workflow from the active path - keep deployment execution in github actions production environment - provision and update a site azure key vault as part of the warm-stack deployment baseline - grant the backend container app managed identity secret data-plane access to that vault during deploy - during deploy, synchronize backend secrets from github production secrets into azure container app secrets via az containerapp secret set - mirror deploy-managed backend secrets into azure key vault during cd so the runtime has a durable vault-backed secret store available from the same release path - inject backend sensitive settings via secretref: environment bindings instead of plain values, including infra-derived azurestorageconnectionstring/azurewebjobsstorage and cosmoskey/cosmosdbkey - inject vault name and uri into backend runtime configuration for server-side user credential custody - keep strict required security preflight validation enabled before rollout ## alternatives considered - keep wrapper + reusable workflow split: - rejected due avoidable operational complexity and slower troubleshooting. - keep plain env injection for sensitive settings: - rejected because azure secret storage + secretref bindings is a stronger default. - skip key vault provisioning until the linked-account runtime rewrite lands: - rejected because it would defer the infrastructure dependency that the server-side credential-custody model already relies on. - move secret sync to ad hoc/manual scripts: - rejected because it increases drift risk and weakens repeatability. ## consequences - positive: - single cd entrypoint is easier to operate and audit, - production secret flow is deterministic from github production to azure runtime, - the backend now receives a ready-to-use key vault for user-held secret custody, - sensitive values are stored in aca secrets and consumed by reference while also being mirrored into key vault. - negative: - cd now owns both infra rollout and secret synchronization responsibilities, - secrets now exist in both aca secret storage and key vault until runtime configuration fully moves behind vault access, - missing required production secrets will block deployment by design. ## related - supersedes deployment-structure aspects of adr 0017. - updates deployment-control reference from adr 0014. ## references - azure container apps secrets: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/manage-secrets - github actions environments: https://docs.github.com/actions/deployment/targeting-different-environments/using-environments-for-deployment - azure key vault secrets: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/secrets/about-secrets

headingSummaries.summary: 1. Add backend lint-fix PR(s) in small slices (functions, middleware, services, utils). 2. Resolve parser project-service coverage for backend test/tooling files. 3. Promote backend lint into root audit:eslint once debt is cleared.

adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0019-phased-backend-lint-hardening.md phased backend lint hardening with deterministic root audits accepted 2026-03-04 context decision follow-up plan context the root audit: scripts in plasius-ltd-site were not reliably enforceable: decision we will enforce deterministic, blocking root audits immediately and phase backend lint debt cleanup as a dedicated follow-up stream. follow-up plan 1. add backend lint-fix pr(s) in small slices (functions, middleware, services, utils). 2. resolve parser project-service coverage for backend test/tooling files. 3. promote backend lint into root audit:eslint once debt is cleared. we will enforce deterministic, blocking root audits immediately and phase backend lint debt cleanup as a dedicated follow-up stream. # adr 0019: phased backend lint hardening with deterministic root audits - status: accepted - date: 2026-03-04 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the root audit: scripts in plasius-ltd-site were not reliably enforceable: - audit:eslint targeted a non-existent root glob and could pass/fail for the wrong reasons. - audit:test invoked root-level vitest directly, which picked up playwright suites and failed for runner-mismatch reasons. - audit:all depended on npm-run-all in a way that was not consistently available from the root package install graph. - audit:npm used || true, so security audit failures were not blocking. at the same time, backend lint strictness currently exposes a large pre-existing debt set that cannot be safely resolved as part of an unrelated release-hardening pass without a focused remediation stream. ## decision we will enforce deterministic, blocking root audits immediately and phase backend lint debt cleanup as a dedicated follow-up stream. root audit gates are now: 1. audit:ts -> root typecheck 2. audit:eslint -> frontend lint (blocking) 3. audit:deps -> dependency tree integrity (npm ls) 4. audit:npm -> blocking npm security audit (no || true) 5. audit:test -> root coverage workflow (test:coverage) backend lint debt is explicitly tracked for a focused cleanup pr sequence that addresses type-safety and parser/project configuration issues without weakening lint rules. ## consequences ### positive - root audit commands now reflect real project quality gates and fail for actionable reasons. - security audit is blocking again. - coverage and typecheck are integrated into the root audit path in a reproducible way. ### negative - backend lint debt remains and is not yet part of root-blocking lint. - a separate cleanup stream is required before backend lint can be promoted into the same blocking gate. ## follow-up plan 1. add backend lint-fix pr(s) in small slices (functions, middleware, services, utils). 2. resolve parser project-service coverage for backend test/tooling files. 3. promote backend lint into root audit:eslint once debt is cleared.

adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0020-cached-graph-middleware-topology-and-availability.md cached graph middleware topology and availability targets accepted 2026-03-05 context decision alternatives considered related decisions context current frontend reads are stable via direct api calls, but this approach is harder to scale and reuse as cross-domain composition grows. we need a stable read architecture that: decision adopt a cached graph middleware layer between clients and backend services. alternatives considered direct client -> services with local client caching: low complexity but weak cross-domain reuse and poor centralized resilience controls. stateful middleware instances with sticky sessions: rejected due to upgrade/failover fragility and uneven scaling. dedi... related decisions adr 0051: service communication patterns - hybrid (pub/sub + orchestration + graphql bff) adr 0014: deploy production on azure container apps (always warm) with redis + cosmos free tier adr 0021: hybrid cache freshness with event-driven updates and ttl safe... adopt a cached graph middleware layer between clients and backend services. # adr 0020: cached graph middleware topology and availability targets - status: accepted - date: 2026-03-05 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context current frontend reads are stable via direct api calls, but this approach is harder to scale and reuse as cross-domain composition grows. we need a stable read architecture that: - supports a client -> middleware -> services model, - keeps middleware stateless where possible, - serves reads during upstream service outages using stale cache data, - tolerates middleware upgrades and cache failovers without user-visible downtime, - scales toward 100k concurrent users. read availability is the top priority. writes may degrade to queued processing during failures. ## decision adopt a cached graph middleware layer between clients and backend services. 1. topology: - client -> graph middleware -> domain services. - clients do not compose service calls directly for graph reads. 2. middleware runtime: - stateless middleware instances, horizontally scaled behind a load balancer. - no in-memory-only authoritative state in middleware processes. - optional short-lived per-instance l1 cache is allowed as a best-effort optimization only. 3. shared cache: - highly replicated distributed redis cache as l2 shared state. - multi-az deployment and automated failover are required. - cache keys and payloads include schema/version metadata for rolling upgrades. 4. availability and deployment model: - zero-downtime deploys for middleware via rolling or blue/green switch-in. - no deploy step may require cache flush as a prerequisite for correctness. - read path may serve stale data during service incidents per freshness policy (see adr 0021). 5. availability targets: - design objective: 99.999% read-path availability. - initial minimum service level: 99.9% while proving production behavior and load envelopes. - system must remain available during routine server updates, service partial outages, and cache failover events. ## alternatives considered - direct client -> services with local client caching: - low complexity but weak cross-domain reuse and poor centralized resilience controls. - stateful middleware instances with sticky sessions: - rejected due to upgrade/failover fragility and uneven scaling. - dedicated graph database as initial mandatory dependency: - deferred to avoid early operational complexity; current services remain source of truth. ## consequences ### positive - centralized read composition, caching, and resilience controls. - better scale characteristics for frontend traffic spikes and repeated read patterns. - deploy and failover behavior is cleaner with stateless middleware. ### negative - extra operational surface (gateway plus distributed cache). - requires strict observability, cache-key governance, and schema/version discipline. - incorrect cache policy can hide upstream correctness issues if not monitored. ## related decisions - adr 0051: service communication patterns - hybrid (pub/sub + orchestration + graphql bff) - adr 0014: deploy production on azure container apps (always warm) with redis + cosmos free tier - adr 0021: hybrid cache freshness with event-driven updates and ttl safety net - adr 0022: queue-first writes with hot-key batching and versioned cache hydration

adrs.summary: Adopt a hybrid cache freshness model:
adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0021-hybrid-cache-freshness-event-driven-with-ttl.md hybrid cache freshness (event-driven with ttl safety net) accepted 2026-03-05 context decision alternatives considered related decisions context we evaluated cache freshness strategies for the cached graph middleware: decision adopt a hybrid cache freshness model: alternatives considered ttl-only: lowest complexity, but unacceptable staleness under frequent writes. event-driven only: best freshness in ideal conditions, but too brittle without ttl fallback. cache miss only (no active refresh): rejected due to latency spikes and weak failover... related decisions adr 0051: service communication patterns - hybrid (pub/sub + orchestration + graphql bff) adr 0020: cached graph middleware topology and availability targets adr 0022: queue-first writes with hot-key batching and versioned cache hydration adopt a hybrid cache freshness model: # adr 0021: hybrid cache freshness (event-driven with ttl safety net) - status: accepted - date: 2026-03-05 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context we evaluated cache freshness strategies for the cached graph middleware: - ttl-only is simple but can leave hot collaborative data stale for too long. - event-driven only is fresh but depends heavily on event pipeline correctness and may degrade badly if events lag or drop. the platform needs high read availability during service failures, with predictable freshness under heavy write activity and localized contention. ## decision adopt a hybrid cache freshness model: 1. primary freshness source: - event-driven invalidation and hydration from service change events. - events are produced via durable outbox and delivered at-least-once. - consumers are idempotent and apply monotonic version checks. 2. safety net: - ttl remains mandatory on all cache entries. - ttl ensures eventual cleanup and recovery from missed/delayed events. 3. freshness semantics per cache entry: - softttl: serve immediately; background refresh permitted. - hardttl: maximum stale serve window during upstream failure. - between softttl and hardttl, middleware may serve stale with revalidation attempts. - after hardttl, entry is no longer eligible for stale-if-error. 4. required cache metadata: - entityid or graph key - fetchedat - softttl and hardttl - version - schemaversion - source 5. baseline freshness tiers: - hot collaborative entities: soft 2s, hard 60s - user/session context: soft 10s, hard 120s - profile/config entities: soft 30s, hard 300s - reference entities: soft 300s, hard 3600s these defaults can be tuned by domain with slo evidence. ## alternatives considered - ttl-only: - lowest complexity, but unacceptable staleness under frequent writes. - event-driven only: - best freshness in ideal conditions, but too brittle without ttl fallback. - cache miss only (no active refresh): - rejected due to latency spikes and weak failover behavior. ## consequences ### positive - better freshness than ttl-only while preserving read continuity during failures. - controlled stale-serving behavior with explicit time windows. - recovery path exists even when event pipeline has transient issues. ### negative - more complexity than single-strategy caching. - requires event contracts, replayability, and lag monitoring. - incorrect version ordering can cause stale overwrite if guards are misimplemented. ## related decisions - status: accepted - date: 2026-03-05 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context read continuity is prioritized, but write behavior must stay responsive at scale and remain correct during outages. expected usage includes high-contention localized updates (for example, many users modifying related chaos-generation nodes at once). a write strategy is needed that: - remains available during dependency failure, - limits lock contention on hot keys, - avoids cache thrash and out-of-order cache corruption, - keeps user-facing write acknowledgement fast. ## decision adopt a queue-first resilient write path with hot-key micro-batching and versioned cache hydration. 1. write ingress modes: - healthy mode: synchronous commit path with bounded latency. - degraded mode: durable queue accept path returning 202 accepted with operationid. 2. ordering and contention control: - partition write processing by entity key or aggregate key. - serialize conflicting updates per partition. - apply optimistic concurrency/version checks at source-of-truth services. 3. hot-key batching: - batch localized high-frequency updates in short windows (target 50-200ms). - domain-specific merge rules compress superseded operations before commit. - batching is adaptive and enabled only where contention merits it. 4. cache hydration after commit: - commit emits versioned change events for cache hydration/invalidation. - middleware cache applies updates only when incoming version is newer. - out-of-order or duplicate events are ignored via idempotency/version guards. 5. write user experience: - default healthy target: fast success response on committed writes. - during failures/overload: deterministic queued response with operation tracking. - clients may poll operation status endpoint for completion when queued. ## alternatives considered - always synchronous writes with no queue fallback: - simpler but fragile under dependency incidents and traffic spikes. - queue everything always: - resilient, but unnecessary consistency delay for low-contention cases. - last-write-wins without ordering/versioning: - high corruption risk for contested entities and out-of-order processing. ## consequences ### positive - better write availability during partial outages. - improved throughput and lower contention on hot collaborative entities. - cache freshness is improved by post-commit hydration events. ### negative - more moving parts (queue, workers, operation status tracking). - event/version contract correctness is critical. - some writes become eventually consistent in degraded mode. ## related decisions - status: accepted - date: 2026-03-05 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the cached graph initiative needs to serve this site now while remaining reusable across other repositories and products. without explicit package boundaries, graph middleware concerns can collapse into a single coupled codebase and become site-specific. we need a package model that: - maps cleanly to solid principles, - minimizes overlap in ownership, - keeps site/runtime concerns separate from graph domain logic, - allows independent package evolution and testing. ## decision adopt the following package split for the cached graph architecture. 1. @plasius/graph-contracts - owns shared schemas and type contracts for graph queries/results, cache metadata, and event payload envelopes. - no runtime side effects, networking, or host dependencies. 2. @plasius/graph-client-core - owns framework-agnostic client query orchestration: request dedupe, normalized client cache, stale policies, and query execution abstraction. - depends on graph-contracts only. 3. @plasius/graph-client-react - owns react-specific bindings for graph-client-core (provider/hooks). - contains no transport/cache engine internals. 4. @plasius/graph-gateway-core - owns read-path graph composition, resolver orchestration, and resilience policy orchestration. - exposes interfaces for cache store, service fetch adapters, and telemetry. - contains no redis/azure-specific code. 5. @plasius/graph-cache-redis - owns redis implementation of gateway cache interfaces. - no query planning/composition logic. 6. @plasius/graph-events - owns event-consumer pipeline for invalidation/hydration and replay/idempotency processing. - no http endpoint ownership. 7. @plasius/graph-write-coordinator - owns queue-first write fallback, hot-key partitioning, and micro-batch orchestration. - no read graph composition ownership. 8. @plasius/graph-runtime-azure-functions - owns azure functions host binding and http surface adaptation for gateway apis. - site/runtime adapter only; no domain orchestration logic. 9. site adapters (inside plasius-ltd-site) - frontend/src/: route/page integration with graph-client-react. - backend/src/: endpoint wiring to graph-runtime-azure-functions. - adapters remain thin and contain site policy only. ## alternatives considered - single monolithic graph package: - rejected due to high coupling and poor reuse across runtimes/frameworks. - only frontend/backend local modules (no publishable packages): - rejected because this locks logic to plasius-ltd-site and duplicates effort for other repos. - runtime-first split (azure-specific packages only): - rejected because cloud/provider coupling would leak into core behavior and reduce portability. ## consequences ### positive - clear ownership and lower risk of cross-cutting overlap. - core graph behavior remains reusable across products and runtimes. - easier ci and release cadence per package responsibility. ### negative - more packages increase release/version management overhead. - interface governance discipline is required to prevent contract drift. ## related decisions - adr 0051: service communication patterns - hybrid (pub/sub + orchestration + graphql bff) - adr 0020: cached graph middleware topology and availability targets - adr 0021: hybrid cache freshness (event-driven with ttl safety net) - adr 0022: queue-first writes, hot-key batching, and versioned cache hydration - adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0024-cached-graph-dependency-inversion-and-adapter-ports.md cached graph dependency inversion and adapter ports accepted 2026-03-05 context decision alternatives considered related decisions context package boundaries alone do not prevent coupling if implementation packages depend directly on infrastructure sdks or site-specific modules. to keep packages independent and reusable, the cached graph system needs explicit dependency-direction rules and ada... decision enforce dependency inversion for the cached graph packages via ports-and-adapters. alternatives considered convention-only architecture (no explicit ports): rejected due to high drift risk under parallel development. core packages importing infrastructure sdks directly: rejected due to portability and testability regression. site-first implementation with later... related decisions adr 0020: cached graph middleware topology and availability targets adr 0021: hybrid cache freshness (event-driven with ttl safety net) adr 0022: queue-first writes, hot-key batching, and versioned cache hydration adr 0023: cached graph package boundaries a... enforce dependency inversion for the cached graph packages via ports-and-adapters. # adr 0024: cached graph dependency inversion and adapter ports - status: accepted - date: 2026-03-05 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context package boundaries alone do not prevent coupling if implementation packages depend directly on infrastructure sdks or site-specific modules. to keep packages independent and reusable, the cached graph system needs explicit dependency-direction rules and adapter ports. ## decision enforce dependency inversion for the cached graph packages via ports-and-adapters. 1. dependency direction - high-level policy packages (graph-client-core, graph-gateway-core, graph-write-coordinator) depend only on interfaces and shared contracts. - infrastructure packages (graph-cache-redis, runtime adapters, queue drivers, telemetry exporters) depend on core package interfaces, never the reverse. - site modules may depend on adapters and cores; cores may not depend on site modules. 2. required core ports - cachestore: get/set/mset/invalidate, ttl controls, compare-and-set/version-aware update. - serviceresolver: fetch by resolver key with typed request/response contracts. - eventpublisher and eventconsumer: publish and consume domain change events with idempotency keys. - writequeue: enqueue/dequeue, partition routing, acknowledgement/retry hooks. - operationstore: query operation status for async write flows. - telemetrysink: metrics/timing/error/tracing hooks. - clock and idgenerator: deterministic testing support. 3. interface segregation rules - read path interfaces are separate from write path interfaces. - event ingestion contracts are separate from event publication contracts. - client transport interface is separate from client cache store interface. 4. substitutability rules - all adapter implementations must preserve core semantic guarantees: - monotonic version application, - idempotent event handling, - stale-if-error eligibility windows from cache metadata, - deterministic operation status transitions. 5. package dependency policy - direct imports from redis/azure/queue sdks are forbidden in graph--core packages. - graph-contracts must remain dependency-light and runtime-agnostic. - cross-package imports must use public export surfaces only. 6. governance - adrs.summary: Adopt a single user capability read path and a richer capability rule model.
adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0025-capabilities-user-scoped-evaluation-and-target-routing.md user-scoped capabilities as the single control surface (with target routing) accepted 2026-03-06 context decision alternatives considered related decisions context feature control is expanding beyond boolean flags. we need one capability model that can: decision adopt a single user capability read path and a richer capability rule model. alternatives considered separate admin capability endpoint (for example /users/me/admin/routes): rejected due to split control-plane reads and duplicated client logic. boolean-only capability model: rejected because rollout and migration flows need pointer/routing behavior and cap... related decisions adr 0051: service communication patterns - hybrid (pub/sub + orchestration + graphql bff) adr 0020: cached graph middleware topology and availability targets adr 0021: hybrid cache freshness (event-driven with ttl safety net) adr 0022: queue-first writes, h... adopt a single user capability read path and a richer capability rule model. # adr 0025: user-scoped capabilities as the single control surface (with target routing) - status: accepted - date: 2026-03-06 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context feature control is expanding beyond boolean flags. we need one capability model that can: - evaluate access at global, role, group, and user scope, - return capability state for any authenticated user, - include admin-only capabilities for admins without introducing a separate admin-only capability-discovery api, - support pointer-style capability values so traffic can be redirected to alternate urls/routes at runtime. the previous approach risked splitting capability discovery into separate paths and coupling admin navigation to a dedicated endpoint. ## decision adopt a single user capability read path and a richer capability rule model. 1. single read contract for users - get /users/me/capabilities/{service} is the capability discovery endpoint for authenticated users. - all user-facing capability evaluation comes from this endpoint, including admin route capabilities (when applicable). - no separate /admin/ discovery endpoint is used for capability reads. 2. admin capabilities are represented as capabilities - admin navigation/access controls are modeled as capability keys (for example admin.route.home). - for non-admin users, admin route capabilities are not present in the returned set. - for admins, admin route capabilities are included in the returned set and may be overridden by scoped rules. 3. capability rules support structured payloads - capability rules support optional payload objects with: - kind (flag | route | url | config) - optional target - optional params (key/value collection for capability-specific configuration) - schemaversion - target can point to internal routes (for example /admin/analytics) or secure external urls (https://...). - payloads are validated and propagated in resolved capabilities for runtime routing and feature behavior selection. 4. capability rules support time windows - capability rules support optional window values: - startsat (inclusive) - endsat (exclusive) - windowed rules are evaluated against server utc time. - if a higher-precedence rule is inactive due to time window, evaluation falls back to lower-precedence active rules. 5. rule management remains admin-only - admins manage rules through: - get /admin/capability-rules - post /admin/capability-rules - delete /admin/capability-rules/{id} - read discovery remains user-scoped; write/admin operations remain admin-scoped. 6. resolution semantics - scope precedence is: user > group > role > global. - optional permission gates (requiredresource + requiredscopes) must pass before a rule can win. - response includes both: - capabilities[] (full metadata, including payload and optional time window) - capabilitymap (boolean fast lookup). - response also includes optional nexttransitionat for upcoming window boundary transitions. ## alternatives considered - separate admin capability endpoint (for example /users/me/admin/routes): - rejected due to split control-plane reads and duplicated client logic. - boolean-only capability model: - rejected because rollout and migration flows need pointer/routing behavior and capability-level parameters. - keep legacy feature-flag-only semantics: - rejected because capabilities now include permissions, scoped policy, and route targeting. ## consequences ### positive - one capability discovery contract for all authenticated users. - admin ux gating and dynamic route targeting use the same primitives as all other capabilities. - cleaner extension path for non-boolean capabilities. ### negative - capability payload and client parsing are more complex than simple flags. - misconfigured targets can cause incorrect routing behavior without strong validation/observability. - windowed rules introduce clock and scheduling complexity; observability and validation are required. ## related decisions - adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0026-profile-account-graph-integration-boundary-rules.md profile/account graph integration boundary rules accepted 2026-03-12 context decision related decisions context adr 0023 and adr 0024 define the generic package split and dependency-inversion rules for the cached graph architecture. they do not yet define the site-local boundaries that must hold while plasius-ltd-site migrates profile and account flows onto those pac... decision adopt a versioned, repo-local boundary policy for profile/account graph integrations at: related decisions adr 0023: cached graph package boundaries and responsibilities adr 0024: cached graph dependency inversion and adapter ports adr 0025: user-scoped capabilities as the single control surface (with target routing) adopt a versioned, repo-local boundary policy for profile/account graph integrations at: # adr 0026: profile/account graph integration boundary rules - status: accepted - date: 2026-03-12 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context adr 0023 and adr 0024 define the generic package split and dependency-inversion rules for the cached graph architecture. they do not yet define the site-local boundaries that must hold while plasius-ltd-site migrates profile and account flows onto those packages. without an explicit repo-level rule set, the migration can drift in two damaging directions: - frontend route modules can keep embedding direct authorizedfetch calls or raw graph transport composition, - backend profile/account handlers can mix site policy, persistence, and graph runtime orchestration in the same module. that would undermine the isolation, reuse, and rollout safety the graph package work is meant to create. ## decision adopt a versioned, repo-local boundary policy for profile/account graph integrations at: - architecture/profile-account-graph-boundary-policy.json this policy is the authoritative rule set for the site repository until superseded. ### frontend boundary rules 1. profile/account route and page modules must consume site-local graph adapters or shared graph hooks. 2. profile/account route and page modules must not build raw graph transport requests inline. 3. profile/account route and page modules must not import backend persistence modules, backend function handlers, or backend graph gateway/runtime packages. 4. shared @plasius/profile components remain ui and state consumers only; site-specific data orchestration stays in site adapters and route composition. ### backend boundary rules 1. profile/account http handlers may depend on site policy helpers and graph runtime adapter entry points. 2. profile/account http handlers must not construct graphgateway or writecoordinator instances inline. 3. persistence access for graph-backed profile/account flows must stay inside backend/src/graph/ adapters or dedicated resolver/commit modules. 4. core graph packages must be imported only through their public export surfaces; infrastructure sdk imports stay inside adapters. ### reference implementation and migration inventory the current admin feature-flag graph path is the site reference implementation for graph adapter structure: - backend/src/graph/feature-flags.graph.ts - backend/src/functions/graph/admin.feature-flags.graph.ts - frontend/src/lib/graph-client.ts - frontend/src/pages/admin/admin-feature-flags-page.tsx current direct-path profile/account modules are migration inventory, not approved templates for new code: - frontend: - frontend/src/context/adminaccesscontext.tsx - frontend/src/pages/admin/admin-users-page.tsx - backend: - backend/src/functions/users/capabilities.ts - backend/src/functions/users/settings.ts - backend/src/functions/users/users.ts ### governance outcome this task defines the rules and records the current legacy direct paths. the follow-on task will consume the same policy artifact to add static checks that block new direct bypass paths in ci. ## consequences ### positive - profile/account migration work now has explicit, reviewable boundaries. - follow-on static enforcement can consume a versioned policy file instead of duplicating rules in code. - legacy direct paths are documented as debt instead of being mistaken for acceptable new patterns. ### negative - the current profile/account implementation still contains direct-path modules until later migration tasks land. - policy maintenance becomes another small governance artifact that must remain synchronized with the codebase. ## related decisions - adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0027-server-side-linked-account-credential-custody.md server-side credential custody and stable user identity for linked accounts accepted 2026-03-21 status tags context decision alternatives considered consequences related decisions references status accepted date: 2026-03-21 version: 1.0 tags security, oauth, profile, identity, linked-accounts, keyvault context the current browser oauth flow still places a signed refreshtoken cookie on the user device and uses the upstream identity-provider subject as the effective user identifier in session refresh paths. decision adopt the following rules for profile and linked-account evolution: alternatives considered keep provider subject as the effective user id: rejected because linking a second provider or changing a primary identity would mutate the user identifier and complicate ownership rules. keep signed refresh tokens in browser cookies: rejected because it exp... consequences positive: account ownership becomes stable across multiple login providers, signing in with any linked provider reaches the same account state instead of creating duplicate profiles, future creator/community connectors can reuse one custody and revocation m... related decisions adr 0015: enforce oauth pkce (s256) for all login attempts adr 0018: single cd workflow with azure secret synchronization and key vault bootstrap adr 0026: profile/account graph integration boundary rules adr 0028: unified account ownership across linked si... references oauth 2.0 security bcp: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9700 azure key vault secrets overview: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/secrets/about-secrets adopt the following rules for profile and linked-account evolution: # adr 0027: server-side credential custody and stable user identity for linked accounts ## status - accepted - date: 2026-03-21 - version: 1.0 ## tags security, oauth, profile, identity, linked-accounts, keyvault ## context the current browser oauth flow still places a signed refreshtoken cookie on the user device and uses the upstream identity-provider subject as the effective user identifier in session refresh paths. that model blocks two requirements: - users must be able to link multiple sign-in identities without their stable user record changing, - linked accounts must grow beyond login providers to creator, streaming, and community platforms such as youtube, twitch, discord, tiktok, kick, and similar destinations. those integrations will involve delegated refresh tokens and account secrets that should not be stored on the user machine. the profile/account surface therefore needs a clear custody rule and a stable identity model before the linked-account surface expands. ## decision adopt the following rules for profile and linked-account evolution: - never store provider refresh tokens or delegated third-party account credentials on the user device, - store user-held delegated credentials only on the server side, using cache for active access and azure key vault for durable custody, - treat userid as a stable internal identifier that is independent of any provider-specific identityid or external account identifier, - treat linked sign-in identities as access paths into the same owned account, not as separate owned accounts, - require any linked sign-in provider to resolve to the same userid, profile, permissions, settings, and downstream linked-account set, - model sign-in identities and creator/community accounts as linked accounts attached to the owning userid, - keep the linked-accounts ui explicit about what is live today versus what is planned next. if browser continuity beyond the short-lived session is required, the browser may hold only an opaque server lookup handle such as an opaque refreshtoken cookie value. it must not hold raw refresh-token material. ## alternatives considered - keep provider subject as the effective user id: - rejected because linking a second provider or changing a primary identity would mutate the user identifier and complicate ownership rules. - keep signed refresh tokens in browser cookies: - rejected because it expands the credential exposure surface and does not meet the desired custody boundary for linked creator/community accounts. - create separate account models for login identities and creator/community integrations: - rejected because it would duplicate lifecycle, audit, and revocation logic around fundamentally similar external-account links. ## consequences - positive: - account ownership becomes stable across multiple login providers, - signing in with any linked provider reaches the same account state instead of creating duplicate profiles, - future creator/community connectors can reuse one custody and revocation model, - delegated credentials move behind server-side controls, auditability, and managed secret storage. - negative: - refresh-token and logout flows must be redesigned around server-side state, - new linked-account entities and deterministic migration logic are required, - legacy cosmos rows keyed by provider subject must be backfilled and then cleaned up after cutover validation, - release infrastructure must provision and expose key vault for the backend. ## related decisions - adr 0015: enforce oauth pkce (s256) for all login attempts - adr 0018: single cd workflow with azure secret synchronization and key vault bootstrap - adr 0026: profile/account graph integration boundary rules - adr 0028: unified account ownership across linked sign-in identities - tdr 0002: linked identity account resolution and legacy cosmos migration ## references - oauth 2.0 security bcp: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9700 - azure key vault secrets overview: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/secrets/about-secrets

adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0028-unified-account-ownership-across-linked-sign-in-identities.md unified account ownership across linked sign-in identities accepted 2026-03-21 status tags context decision alternatives considered consequences related decisions references status accepted date: 2026-03-21 version: 1.0 tags identity, oauth, profile, migration, cosmos, linked-accounts context the current login model still treats the upstream provider subject as the effective owner identifier across session, profile, permission, and linked-account flows. decision adopt the following ownership rule: alternatives considered keep one profile per provider identity: rejected because it violates the intended linked-account product behavior and creates duplicate ownership state. treat "link" as a frontend affordance only and reconcile accounts manually later: rejected because it wo... consequences positive: linked google/apple/microsoft identities become interchangeable access paths to the same account, profile/account features can be designed around one owner model instead of provider-specific branches, delegated creator/community integrations inher... related decisions adr 0015: enforce oauth pkce (s256) for all login attempts adr 0027: server-side credential custody and stable user identity for linked accounts tdr 0001: profile linked-account credential custody tdr 0002: linked identity account resolution and legacy cosm... references oauth 2.0 security bcp: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9700 azure cosmos db design patterns: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/nosql/modeling-data adopt the following ownership rule: # adr 0028: unified account ownership across linked sign-in identities ## status - accepted - date: 2026-03-21 - version: 1.0 ## tags identity, oauth, profile, migration, cosmos, linked-accounts ## context the current login model still treats the upstream provider subject as the effective owner identifier across session, profile, permission, and linked-account flows. that means: - a google login and an apple login naturally become different effective users, - a later "link" action behaves like another login path rather than a true account-link operation, - the same person can be shown different profiles depending on which provider they used to sign in, - migrating to creator/community integrations would compound the ownership problem because delegated account links would hang off unstable provider-scoped identifiers. the desired product behavior is stricter than "stable ids eventually exist." once multiple sign-in identities are linked, it must not matter which linked provider the person uses to access the account. they must reach the same owned account state. ## decision adopt the following ownership rule: - userid is the canonical owned account identifier for profile, permissions, settings, linked accounts, and session ownership, - identityid is a provider-scoped sign-in identity record linked to exactly one owning userid, - logging in through any linked sign-in identity must resolve the same owning userid, - primary identity selection changes notification/display preference and recovery posture, not account ownership, - creator/community connectors are linked to the same owning userid, regardless of which sign-in provider created them, - legacy provider-subject-keyed cosmos rows must be migrated into stable account ownership; they must not remain the long-term source of truth, - migration must be additive first, then cleanup-driven after validation; do not perform a blanket cosmos wipe to force correctness. ## alternatives considered - keep one profile per provider identity: - rejected because it violates the intended linked-account product behavior and creates duplicate ownership state. - treat "link" as a frontend affordance only and reconcile accounts manually later: - rejected because it would create silent data divergence in profile, permissions, and downstream connectors. - purge all legacy cosmos identity/profile data before rollout: - rejected because it destroys legitimate early-user data and removes the ability to validate migration correctness against prior state. ## consequences - positive: - linked google/apple/microsoft identities become interchangeable access paths to the same account, - profile/account features can be designed around one owner model instead of provider-specific branches, - delegated creator/community integrations inherit one durable ownership model. - negative: - auth callback, refresh, /oauth/me, bootstrap, and self-service profile routes all need ownership refactoring, - cosmos data keyed by legacy provider subjects requires backfill and cleanup tooling, - legacy session formats must be versioned and cut over with forced re-authentication where needed. ## related decisions - tdr 0002: linked identity account resolution and legacy cosmos migration ## references - oauth 2.0 security bcp: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9700 - azure cosmos db design patterns: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/nosql/modeling-data

status: accepted - date: 2026-03-28 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context adr 0028 established that owned account state must hang off a stable userid, not whichever upstream provider subject happened to create the profile first. that decision left one important delivery gap in plasius-ltd-site: - the profile surface still lacked a documented graph contract for listing and mutating linked sign-in identities, - primary identity changes could drift if multiple rows tried to own "primary" state independently, - link and switch requests needed stronger reliability and security controls because users can naturally double-submit account actions from the browser, - rollout needed to stay reversible while the frontend still exposes direct oauth link affordances instead of a graph-backed linked-identity ui. this work also has explicit non-functional requirements: - authorization must be enforced on every linked-identity read and mutation, - repeated submissions must stay idempotent and avoid retry amplification, - identity displays must minimize sensitive data exposure, - package boundaries must continue to prefer public graph/runtime packages while keeping site-specific contracts local until a reusable surface is justified. ## decision 1. add the linked-identity graph contract in the site backend: - profile.identities.read - profile.linked-identity:link - profile.linked-identity:unlink - profile.linked-identity:set-primary 2. gate the linked-identity graph surface behind a dedicated site flag: - plasius-ltd-site introduces profile.linked-identities.enabled. - the flag defaults to disabled unless explicitly enabled by environment override or feature-flag state. 3. keep owned-account primary state authoritative in one row: - accountsentity.primaryidentityid is the source of truth. - read models derive each linked identity's primary boolean from that account row. - write paths do not attempt distributed multi-row "primary" updates across linked identities. 4. enforce self-service and reliability controls at the graph boundary: - target userid and actorid must match the authenticated owned account, - unlink rejects removal of the last remaining sign-in identity, - unlink rejects removal of the current primary identity until another primary is chosen, - graph idempotency keys are the replay-safety mechanism for repeated link and primary-switch submissions. 5. minimize identity disclosure in read payloads: - provider email is exposed when already present on the linked identity, - otherwise the provider subject is masked before it leaves the backend. ## consequences ### positive - linked-identity operations now have a documented and test-pinned graph contract. - primary identity consistency no longer depends on keeping several cosmos rows perfectly synchronized. - rollout stays reversible with a dedicated kill switch independent of the broader profile/account graph flag. - security and reliability requirements are exercised with focused graph, contract, and security acceptance tests. ### negative - the linked-identity surface is temporarily backend-only until the profile ui adopts it. - the account row and linked identity rows can still contain an advisory primary boolean that is no longer authoritative. - site-local adapter code is required for rollout control and identifier masking because the contract is still application-specific. ## related decisions - adr 0007: decouple auth/profile consumption from monorepo workspace builds - adr 0026: profile/account graph integration boundary rules - adr 0028: unified account ownership across linked sign-in identities - adr 0029: shared profile validation behind a site rollout flag - tdr 0002: linked identity account resolution and legacy cosmos migration
