status: accepted - date: 2026-03-29 ## context story #484 extends the linked-accounts surface beyond login providers. the site ui already distinguishes live sign-in identities from planned creator/community connectors, but that distinction was still backed by a hard-coded frontend list. that left three gaps: - the owned-account backend had no concrete provider catalog for creator, streaming, community, and promotion connectors, - the frontend could not consume purpose, scope, credential-custody, or audit metadata from the backend contract, - the richer catalog would have to ship all at once unless it had its own rollout seam. this work also had to respect adr 0007: if a reusable package boundary is not real yet, do not create a fake one just to move code around. shared primitives should continue to come from published @plasius/ packages, but site-specific linked-account behavior should stay in the site until another runtime proves the boundary. ## decision adopt the following approach for the creator/community expansion: 1. extend the existing linked-identity read envelope with a linkedaccounts catalog array that includes: - provider label, - purpose and surface metadata, - requested/granted scopes, - credential strategy and token-status metadata, - audit-action coverage, - connection status for live or planned connectors. 2. keep the richer creator/community catalog rendering behind vitelinkedaccountcatalogenabled so the current linked-identities ui can remain stable while rollout happens. 3. expand the site-local linked-account entity model to support non-login connectors with purpose, scope, connection-state, and credential metadata. 4. emit audit-safe backend events for the link, unlink, and primary-promotion actions that are live today, while publishing reconnect expectations in the provider catalog for future non-login connectors. 5. do not extract a new npm package yet. the site remains the only runtime that consumes this catalog contract today, so package extraction would create a maintenance boundary without a second consumer to justify it. ## consequences - positive: - sign-in identities and creator/community connectors now share one owned-account catalog model, - the frontend can render provider purpose, scope, and credential-custody metadata from backend-owned data instead of static copy, - rollout remains reversible without disabling the whole linked-identities ui, - audit expectations are explicit for live and planned connector actions. - negative: - the linked-identity read envelope grows beyond the original minimal list shape, - there is temporary duplication between the existing fallback planned-copy path and the rollout-gated catalog renderer, - a future second consumer may still justify extracting a reusable package once the boundary becomes real. ## related decisions - status: accepted - date: 2026-04-01 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the moderator route already exists in the admin shell, but story f33.s1 adds materially new behavior: - transcript evidence with participant and timestamp context, - annotation capture tied to moderation policy references, - privacy-sensitive transcript segments that require stricter handling than standard moderation copy, - a need to disable the new evidence-review workflow quickly without removing the broader moderation route. this story also carries explicit nfr-privacy requirements. the rollout model therefore needs to answer two separate concerns: - who may reach the moderation route at all, - whether the new evidence-review workspace should be active for the current environment or cohort. ## decision 1. keep route access capability-driven: - the existing admin.route.moderation capability continues to control whether moderator or service-admin users can reach /admin/moderation. 2. gate the new evidence-review workflow with a dedicated server-side feature flag: - plasius-ltd-site introduces admin.moderation.review.enabled, - the backend moderation workspace evaluates the flag per site partition and current user affinities, - the moderation page consumes the backend workspace response instead of duplicating rollout logic in frontend env flags. 3. enforce transcript minimization on the server: - standard moderator sessions receive redacted sensitive segments, - privileged review requires explicit server-recognized affinity such as service-admin or moderation-sensitive-review, - frontend rendering receives already-minimized transcript text and only displays reveal state metadata. 4. keep the moderation evidence contract site-local for now: - the workspace payload and annotation record shape live inside plasius-ltd-site, - no new public package is introduced until a second runtime needs the same moderation review model. ## consequences ### positive - the new moderation evidence workflow is remotely reversible without redeploying the whole admin shell. - route access and feature rollout remain distinct, which keeps capability semantics stable. - privacy controls are centralized server-side rather than relying on client discipline. - moderation annotations can be tested and evolved without forcing a new public package boundary early. ### negative - /admin/moderation can remain visible while the evidence workspace itself is disabled, so the page must preserve a useful fallback state. - sensitive transcript reveal now depends on explicit affinity naming and operator configuration. - the moderation evidence payload is currently site-local and may need later extraction if additional services adopt it. ## related decisions - status: accepted - date: 2026-04-08 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context adr 0030 introduced linked-identity graph operations behind profile.linked-identities.enabled, but story f16.s3 adds security and operational requirements that cut across several existing subsystems: - primary sign-in identity changes must notify the previous primary email address, - link, unlink, and set-primary mutations must leave tamper-evident evidence that operators can query later, - rapid identity churn must be bounded across direct self-service, oauth callback, and graph mutation entry points, - discoverability remains capability-led, so this story should not introduce a new frontend-only gate. the repo already has a tamper-evident audit store and a durable notification outbox. the main design question is whether linked-identity security events should reuse those planes or create feature-local audit/notification machinery. ## decision 1. reuse the existing linked-identity rollout gates: - keep profile.linked-identities.enabled as the parent rollout flag, - keep profile.linked-identities.self-service.enabled as the direct self-service mutation gate, - do not add a frontend-only flag for linked-account discoverability. 2. record linked-identity mutations in the shared tamper-evident audit store: - emit the family profile.linked-identity.update, - reuse the existing audit envelope and retention policy, - represent self-service callers as actortype: "end-user" from source.surface: "public-api", - carry direct-vs-callback-vs-graph provenance in details.deliverypath. 3. reuse the existing notification outbox for primary-identity change warnings: - enqueue the new notification type primary-identity-change, - target the previous primary email address, - carry templateid = "primary-identity-change-email" plus locale metadata for downstream delivery handling, - surface failures through the existing admin notification report and slos. 4. apply one shared mutation throttle across all linked-identity write entry points: - persist per-user mutation budget in table storage, - evaluate the same throttle in oauth callback, direct self-service routes, and graph writes, - return an explicit 429 with retryafterseconds when the budget is exhausted. 5. keep the implementation site-local for now: - the audit family, throttle record, and notification payload stay inside plasius-ltd-site, - no new public npm package is introduced until a second runtime needs the same linked-identity security plane. ## consequences ### positive - operators keep one queryable tamper-evident audit plane for both admin actions and linked-identity security events. - delivery failures for primary-identity warnings automatically appear in the existing notification dashboard, alerts, and reconciliation flow. - abuse throttling stays consistent regardless of whether a mutation arrived through oauth callback, direct http, or graph write. - rollback remains simple because the story reuses the existing linked-identity feature flags instead of introducing another control plane. ### negative - the shared admin-audit store now contains end-user initiated security events, so docs and validators must distinguish actor/source semantics clearly. - graph clients must preserve caller-visible 429 responses instead of treating them as transport dependency failures. - email delivery still depends on the existing outbox provider abstraction rather than a dedicated linked-identity mailer. ## related decisions - adr 0025: capabilities user-scoped evaluation and target routing - adr 0028: unified account ownership across linked sign-in identities - adr 0030: linked-identity graph operations behind a dedicated rollout flag - adr 0031: linked-account catalog rollout and provider metadata

status: proposed - date: 2026-04-09 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the current translation contract is flat: - the backend serves get /i18n/{language}, - blob storage is organised as flat locale files such as en-gb.json, - @plasius/translations expects one language dictionary per fetch. that model does not align with the required operating mode where the site should load translation json for the current page from: - /language/language-code/translation-path.json the site also needs a stable default locale of en-gb, a durable fallback chain, and the ability to fetch only the bundles needed for the current route and shared shell. ## decision 1. replace the flat runtime contract with a page-scoped backend contract: - get /language/{language}/{translationpath} 2. store translation assets by locale plus logical path: - {language}/frontend/app-shell.json - {language}/frontend/routes/about.json - {language}/frontend/routes/admin/home.json 3. treat en-gb as the canonical baseline locale and final fallback for every translation path. 4. keep translation-path naming logical and stable: - paths represent ui ownership boundaries such as app shell, route, or shared component, - paths do not need to mirror the physical source tree exactly. 5. upgrade the admin translation upload path to accept nested translation paths so authoring and delivery use the same storage model. ## consequences ### positive - the site can fetch only the bundles needed for the current surface. - translation ownership becomes clearer by route and shared component boundary. - the backend contract matches the required /language/language/path.json delivery model. - en-gb becomes an explicit, durable fallback instead of a mix of en and locale-specific defaults. ### negative - the translation package and frontend integration both need api changes to support multiple bundle loads. - operators must manage more files than a single flat locale asset. - the backend upload and validation path becomes more complex because nested logical paths must be accepted safely. ## related decisions - status: proposed - date: 2026-04-09 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context large parts of the site still render english copy directly from frontend components, route files, dialog definitions, and backend responses surfaced to the ui. that prevents the translation service from being the single source of truth for visible copy. the requirement for this migration is stronger than "support translated pages." the requirement is: - aria-label and tooltip text, - loading and empty states, - confirmation copy, - validation and error messages that currently arrive from the backend as english prose. ## decision 1. all user-visible copy rendered by the site frontend must resolve through @plasius/translations. 2. raw frontend string literals are not allowed for user-visible copy outside these exceptions: - developer diagnostics, - test fixtures, - telemetry identifiers that are not shown to end users. 3. shared ui surfaces such as shell navigation, auth menus, profile editors, and destructive confirmations must own translation bundles just like route pages. 4. backend apis whose messages are rendered directly in the ui must return stable message keys or codes plus interpolation arguments, not english prose intended for direct display. 5. accessibility copy is part of the translation obligation and must be migrated with the visible ui. ## consequences ### positive - accessibility surfaces remain aligned with the visible language of the page. ### negative - existing ui tests that assert raw english text will need to be rewritten around translation fixtures. - some backend handlers need contract changes because they currently emit user-facing prose. - developers must maintain translation keys and bundle ownership as part of normal ui work. ## related decisions - adr 0034: serve page-scoped language bundles from the backend - adr 0036: translation rollout, governance, and validation gates

status: accepted - date: 2026-04-09 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context this localization migration spans a shared package, backend delivery routes, admin upload tooling, public routes, admin routes, shared components, and backend-originated ui messages. shipping it as one undifferentiated change would make rollback and operational verification difficult. repo policy also requires every feature to have a named remotely controllable feature flag before implementation starts, and the completion criteria for user-facing work already require documentation, tests, and release-quality validation. ## decision 1. split delivery across explicit feature flags: - site.i18n.page-bundles.enabled - site.i18n.frontend-consumption.enabled - site.i18n.localization-governance.enabled 2. treat en-gb translation completeness as the release baseline: - no route is considered migrated until its en-gb bundle exists, - fallback behaviour must be tested at the bundle-path level. 3. add migration governance for translation ownership: - each route declares the bundles it consumes, - shared components declare or inherit their bundle ownership, - backend ui message contracts document the translation keys they emit. 4. add validation gates for: - missing bundle handling, - en-gb fallback behaviour, - representative translated rendering for public and admin routes, - accessibility label coverage for migrated surfaces. 5. keep operator authoring and upload aligned with the runtime path model so translation completeness can be audited against actual bundle paths. 6. keep a machine-readable governance inventory in architecture/localization-governance-policy.json, and validate it through npm run audit:policy so ownership, representative en-gb bundle fixtures, and required documentation drift cannot land silently. ## consequences ### positive - status: accepted - date: 2026-04-09 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the legacy delete-user compatibility path in plasius-ltd-site only soft-deleted the userentity. that left three gaps for feature #19 / story #37: - there was no account-level lifecycle record carrying the 30-day hard-delete deadline, - authenticated sessions and linked-identity sign-ins could still succeed because auth did not consult an owned-account deletion state, - deletion requests were not written to the shared audit plane with an explicit retention classification. this work also has explicit non-functional requirements: - account deletion must be auditable and privacy-safe, - repeated delete requests must be idempotent, - rollout must stay reversible without redeploying unrelated auth/profile code, - already deleted accounts must stay blocked even if rollout for new delete requests is paused. ## decision 1. add a site-local rollout flag for the new lifecycle path: - plasius-ltd-site introduces account.soft-delete.lifecycle.enabled, - the normal production control plane is the stored featureflagentity, - accountsoftdeletelifecycleenabled remains a break-glass or local-development override. 2. make accountsentity the lifecycle source of truth for account deletion: - account records now carry deletionstate, deletionrequestedat, deletionrequestedby, harddeleteat, and retentionpolicytag, - the delete compatibility route soft-deletes the account record and still soft-deletes the userentity so legacy list/read paths stop surfacing the profile. 3. enforce deletion at authentication time: - internal session validation and provider-login flows now reject accounts whose accountsentity state is soft-deleted, - disabling the rollout flag stops new soft-delete transitions but does not silently restore already deleted accounts. 4. keep audit evidence on the shared tamper-evident audit plane: - deletion requests emit profile.account.delete events through writeadminauditevent, - retention class is admin-security, - details remain privacy-safe and carry only lifecycle metadata such as harddeleteat, idempotent, and the retention-policy tag. 5. expose the self-service delete control through a composed backend capability: - the frontend consumes profile.action.delete-account from get /api/users/me/capabilities/frontend, - the backend emits that capability only while account.soft-delete.lifecycle.enabled resolves to enabled, - the rollout flag stays the operator kill switch and the capability stays the frontend discoverability gate for the profile settings action. ## consequences ### positive - account deletion now has a durable lifecycle record and a scheduled hard-delete timestamp. - auth/session enforcement now matches the stored account state instead of relying only on route-level deletes. - rollout is reversible for new delete requests through a documented feature flag. - the profile page now relies on a backend-emitted capability instead of a frontend-local toggle to decide whether the delete action is discoverable. - audit evidence for deletion requests is consistent with the rest of the shared admin-security event stream. ### negative - the site now owns another rollout-control evaluator and account-lifecycle helper. - rollback only stops new lifecycle transitions; operators must explicitly restore an account if they need to undo a prior soft-delete. - the delete-account ui now depends on both the lifecycle rollout flag and the synthesized capability contract, so rollout debugging spans both layers. - the compatibility delete route remains dual-path while the flag is still disabled in some environments. ## related decisions - adr 0025: user-scoped capabilities as the single control surface (with target routing) - adr 0028: unified account ownership across linked sign-in identities - adr 0033: linked-identity security events in the shared audit and notification plane

status: accepted - date: 2026-04-03 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context roadmap feature #176 and story #198 require the repo to move beyond an inline ci shell check for combined coverage. the existing state had three gaps: - the 80% threshold lived only in ci shell code instead of a versioned policy artifact, - profile/account critical-path suites existed, but the required unit, integration, accessibility, and e2e evidence was not documented as one reviewable matrix, - ci uploaded raw coverage to codecov, but did not publish a retained diff-coverage report that explains whether changed profile/account source files kept their own coverage healthy. the repo still needs an operational escape hatch because github actions cannot query the site feature-flag service directly during ci execution. ## decision 1. version the profile/account testing gate as source: - architecture/profile-account-testing-quality-policy.json now records the thresholds, critical-path matrix, evidence outputs, and rollback posture for this feature. 2. keep the parent feature flag explicit: - feature #176 uses profile.account.testing-quality-gates.enabled as its named rollout control, - github actions mirrors that control with the break-glass env override profileaccounttestingqualitygatesenabled. 3. enforce coverage from a node tool instead of inline shell logic: - the repo now computes combined, per-workspace, and changed-file coverage from coverage/combined/lcov.info, - changed frontend/src/ and backend/src/ files must appear in the report and meet the committed threshold. 4. treat critical-path drift as policy drift: - the committed matrix references the blocking ci steps that already run the critical-path suites, - validator tests fail if the matrix, evidence files, or ci workflow steps drift apart. 5. publish retained evidence for review: - ci now writes a policy-backed coverage report and uploads a testing-quality evidence bundle for later audit and review. ## consequences ### positive - coverage thresholds and critical-path expectations are now reviewable source artifacts. - ci failures explain whether the regression is global coverage, workspace coverage, changed-file coverage, or matrix drift. - story #198 now has retained evidence instead of only transient workflow logs. - the break-glass path is explicit and test-covered instead of being an undocumented ci edit. ### negative - ci retains one more artifact bundle and executes one more policy-backed enforcement step. - the break-glass env override still exists because ci cannot consume the live feature-flag service directly. - adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0041-profile-mfa-step-up-composed-rollout-gate.md profile mfa step-up behind a composed rollout gate accepted 2026-04-13 context decision consequences related decisions context roadmap feature #17 adds two distinct requirements to the self-service profile surface: decision adopt a composed gate for profile mfa step-up: consequences positive: frontend discoverability and backend enforcement stay aligned through one composed contract, rollout remains reversible without a code redeploy, self-service mutation paths fail closed and still preserve explicit bounded errors for invalid or expi... related decisions adr 0025: capabilities are user-scoped evaluation and target routing adr 0026: profile/account graph integration boundary rules adr 0029: shared profile validation behind a site rollout flag adr 0030: linked-identity graph operations behind a dedicated roll... adopt a composed gate for profile mfa step-up: # adr 0041: profile mfa step-up behind a composed rollout gate - status: accepted - date: 2026-04-13 ## context roadmap feature #17 adds two distinct requirements to the self-service profile surface: - users need a discoverable mfa enrollment and management experience inside profile settings, - profile mutations must require a short-lived mfa step-up when mfa is enabled. that requirement crosses both product access and operational rollout concerns. if the frontend showed mfa controls from a local env flag, discoverability could drift from the backend. if the backend enforced step-up without a dedicated rollback seam, operators would have to choose between shipping blind or redeploying to recover from an outage. the implementation also has to satisfy the repo's standing rules: - capabilities are the primary frontend-facing access contract, - every feature still needs a remotely controllable feature flag, - self-service profile mutation checks must fail closed and be re-validated on the backend, - site-local behavior should stay in plasius-ltd-site until a second runtime proves that a reusable package boundary is real. ## decision adopt a composed gate for profile mfa step-up: 1. use profile.mfa.step-up.enabled as the backend-authoritative rollout flag. - profilemfastepupenabled remains the break-glass or local-development env override. - the default posture is disabled unless the feature flag or override enables it. 2. emit profile.mfa.settings only when the rollout flag is enabled and the mfa encryption key is configured. - frontend discoverability and settings rendering consume the capability, not a frontend-only env flag. - the backend remains responsible for composing flag state into the emitted capability. 3. enforce step-up on every self-service profile mutation boundary. - graph-backed profile writes must require a verified mfa challenge, - legacy compatibility mutations for self-service user and settings updates must require the same challenge, - the frontend blocks the final save locally, but the backend still rejects bypass attempts with stable mfa error codes. 4. keep factor material and challenge handling site-local for now. - no new @plasius/ package is extracted yet because plasius-ltd-site is still the only runtime using this mfa contract. 5. define operator rollback and outage behavior around the flag, not a bypass. - if mfa endpoints or dependencies degrade, disable profile.mfa.step-up.enabled to suppress the capability and enforcement, - do not allow the frontend or backend to silently skip mfa while the flag remains enabled. ## consequences - positive: - frontend discoverability and backend enforcement stay aligned through one composed contract, - rollout remains reversible without a code redeploy, - self-service mutation paths fail closed and still preserve explicit bounded errors for invalid or expired challenges, - the operator-facing rollback path is documented and testable. - negative: - the backend owns extra composition logic because the capability depends on rollout and runtime-secret readiness, - profile saves now depend on mfa status and challenge endpoints being healthy while the flag is enabled, - a future shared mfa package may still be justified if another runtime needs the same contract. ## related decisions - adr 0025: capabilities are user-scoped evaluation and target routing - adr 0026: profile/account graph integration boundary rules - adr 0029: shared profile validation behind a site rollout flag - adr 0030: linked-identity graph operations behind a dedicated rollout flag

proposed → accepted - date: 2025-09-12 - version: 1.0 - supersedes: n/a - superseded by: n/a --- ## tags infra, hosting, cloud, scalability, costs --- ## context we need to decide whether to deploy our infrastructure in the public cloud or manage it on on-premises servers. key factors include: - scalability: need to handle growth from 100 → 1,000,000 users. - reliability: users expect uptime close to 99.9%. - cost profile: balance between early mvp (low burn rate) and scale-up. - devops velocity: single founder initially, small team later. - integration with github ci/cd, affiliate apis, and azure-native services (e.g., key vault, container apps, static web apps). --- ## decision we will adopt cloud hosting as our deployment model and select azure as our primary cloud provider. this decision reflects a preference for leveraging managed cloud services to achieve scalability, reliability, and operational efficiency, rather than maintaining on-premises infrastructure. choosing azure as the primary provider is based on its strong integration with our existing toolchain and regional presence, while maintaining a commitment to designing our architecture to remain as cloud-agnostic as possible to allow future migration between cloud providers if needed. --- ## alternatives considered - on-premises / self-hosted hardware - pros: full control over data and infrastructure; potentially lower costs at very large scale. - cons: high upfront capital expenditure; requires dedicated operations team; limited scalability; slower time-to-market. - azure (primary cloud provider) - pros: deep integration with github actions and microsoft ecosystem; strong regional presence in uk south; rich managed services; good developer experience. - cons: some degree of vendor lock-in; potentially higher costs compared to bare-metal at scale. - aws - pros: largest cloud provider with broadest global coverage and mature service portfolio. - cons: less seamless integration with github actions compared to azure; regional presence considerations. - google cloud platform (gcp) - pros: strong data analytics and machine learning services; competitive pricing. - cons: smaller market share; fewer managed services aligned with our stack; regional availability. - oracle cloud - pros: competitive pricing on certain workloads; strong database offerings. - cons: less mature ecosystem; limited community support; smaller regional footprint. --- ## consequences - positive: - fast time-to-market with managed cloud services. - elastic scalability and pay-as-you-grow pricing. - reduced operational burden for a small founding team. - ability to leverage cloud provider ecosystems and integrations. - negative: - potential cloud provider lock-in, mitigated by designing for portability. - higher per-unit costs compared to owning hardware at very large scale. - dependence on internet connectivity for access to infrastructure. - risks/trade-offs: - long-term costs may exceed on-premises at very large scale. - need to continuously monitor and control cloud spending. - commitment to cloud-agnostic design increases initial complexity but enables future migration flexibility. --- ## related decisions - adr-0048 (future): choice of azure container apps vs aks for service orchestration. - adr-0049 (future): multi-cloud vs single-cloud strategy. --- ## references - azure container apps overview - azure static web apps documentation - adr-0043: frontend hosting — containerized vs non-container models ## status - proposed → accepted - date: 2025-09-12 - version: 1.0 - supersedes: n/a - superseded by: n/a ## tags frontend, hosting, containers, aca, portability, devops, cicd, edge ## context we need to select a frontend hosting model that fits our goals of agnostic architecture and portable deployments. the primary decision is between: - containerized frontend hosting: shipping the next.js frontend as an oci image, enabling deployments across any container platform. - non-container hosting models: using platform-native options that do not require a container image, such as static site hosts or managed frontend platforms. key drivers for this decision: - portability: ability to deploy the same artifact across different environments/clouds. - operational control: full control of the runtime, middleware, and deployment process. - consistency: aligning frontend and backend deployment/release models. - flexibility for future needs: ssr, custom middleware, or advanced routing. ## decision adopt a containerized frontend as our hosting model. ## alternatives considered ### a) azure static web apps (swa) non-container hosting option. - pros - excellent developer experience: pr previews, global edge, built-in auth providers. - low cost at low traffic; minimal ops. - cons - less control over ssr/runtime; multi-region behaviour is opinionated. - artifact is not a generic container (less portable across clouds/on-prem). ### b) vercel / netlify / cloudflare pages non-container hosting options. - pros - best-in-class dx, previews, edge functions, global distribution. - cons - vendor-specific platform features increase lock-in; not a portable container. - pricing can escalate with edge function usage. ### c) app service (web apps) non-container hosting option. - pros - familiar azure service, supports web app deployments, deployment slots. - cons - less flexibility and portability compared to container-based approaches. - may not align with container-based workflows and operational models. ## portability & agnosticism guarantees - single artifact: frontend ships as an oci image; no platform‑specific code paths. - ingress neutrality: standard http(s); no aca‑specific apis in app code. - state externalised: no reliance on local disk; asset storage via cdn/object storage; environment via 12‑factor config. - observability: use opentelemetry (where applicable) and standard logs so backends (log analytics/datadog/otlp) are swappable. - build modes: support both ssr and static export builds so we can move between aca, swa, or other hosts with minimal change. ## deployment & release (non‑binding outline) - build container in github actions → push to acr → update aca revision. - blue/green rollout using aca revisions; ability to pin % traffic during canary. - rollback by re‑activating previous revision. ## consequences - positive - uniform deployment model (containers) across frontend and backend; simpler mental model. - easy rollbacks and reproducible builds; improved portability. - room for advanced ssr/middleware use‑cases without platform constraints. - negative / risks - lose some swa niceties (automatic pr previews, global edge distribution by default). - need to add cdn/waf later if global latency or security requires it. - containerized ssr can be more expensive than purely static hosting at low traffic. ## revisit criteria - if operational cost at low traffic exceeds budget without offsetting benefits, reconsider swa for static export. - if we require global edge execution for middleware/functions, evaluate cloudflare/vercel with portability strategy. - if aca feature limits block required routing/security features, revisit app service or aks. ## related decisions - adr‑0001: cloud vs on‑prem (cloud → azure) - adr‑0006: cicd - adr-0050: runtime/container orchestration choices (separate adr) ## database — choose postgresql for primary oltp store ## status - proposed → accepted - date: 2025-09-12 - version: 1.0 - supersedes: n/a - superseded by: n/a ## tags database, postgres, persistence, portability, ol tp, azure, relational, jsonb, cost ## context we need a primary online transactional processing (oltp) database for user accounts, preferences, feedback signals, workflow metadata (n8n), and affiliate click/attribution logs. our pillars require platform/vendor agnosticism and data portability. the database should: - be widely supported across clouds and on‑prem. - offer acid transactions, strong consistency, and mature tooling. - support both structured and semi‑structured data (e.g., product facets, preferences). - provide managed options on azure today, with easy migration paths elsewhere later. - keep total cost of ownership low for mvp, with a path to scale (read replicas, partitioning). ## decision adopt postgresql as the primary oltp database (managed on azure today: azure database for postgresql flexible server), with a schema that favors portability (standard sql, minimal engine‑specific features). ### portability & data commitments - use standard sql and avoid proprietary features; limit extensions to commonly portable ones. - permit jsonb for semi‑structured fields (e.g., vendor attributes) while keeping core entities normalized. - prefer portable extensions only when justified (e.g., pgtrgm for text search; pgcrypto for hashing). avoid tight coupling to non‑portable extensions. - backups and exports must be standard pgdump / logical replication to ease migration. - store large binaries in object storage (blob/s3‑compatible) rather than the db. - maintain data‑retention and gdpr portability (export/delete) by design. ## alternatives considered ### a) azure cosmos db (core/sql, mongo api, cassandra) - pros - global distribution, multi‑region writes, low‑latency geo‑replication. - serverless pricing models for spiky workloads. - cons - higher lock‑in to azure; query model and ru pricing are platform‑specific. - oltp relational modeling and joins are limited; portability lower than postgres. - migration off cosmos is non‑trivial. ### b) azure sql database (managed sql server) - pros - mature managed service; strong tooling and performance. - good for relational workloads, familiar to many teams. - cons - less portable across clouds/on‑prem compared to postgres. - licensing/cost considerations at scale; fewer open‑source extensions. ### c) mysql (managed variants) - pros - widely available and portable; good performance for simple oltp. - cons - weaker json features vs postgres jsonb; fewer advanced indexing options. - extension ecosystem thinner; less flexible for analytics/search add‑ons. ### d) mongodb / document stores (atlas or cosmos mongo api) - pros - flexible schema; good fit for irregular product catalogs. - cons - eventual consistency modes and document‑first model complicate transactions and joins. - affiliate attribution, preferences, and reporting benefit from relational integrity. - portability impacted by server features and provider choice. ### e) self‑hosted postgres on vms/containers - pros - maximum control; can run anywhere; no vendor limits. - cons - higher ops burden (ha, backups, patching, monitoring). not ideal for solo founder mvp. ### f) serverless/backend‑as‑a‑service (e.g., supabase, firebase) - pros - faster to bootstrap; auth + storage included (supabase uses postgres). - cons - tighter platform coupling; may constrain networking and scaling choices. - for firebase (non‑sql), portability is weaker. ## consequences - positive - high portability: postgres is ubiquitous on azure/aws/gcp/on‑prem. - strong feature set: acid, jsonb, indexing, ctes, views; ecosystem of drivers/orms. - managed option on azure reduces ops for mvp while keeping migration paths open. - works well with n8n (officially supported) and our analytics/export needs. - negative / risks - if we need active‑active multi‑region writes with sub‑100ms rpo/rto, postgres becomes complex; cosmos‑class systems excel here. - at very large scale, tuning/partitioning and read replicas will be required; adds operational complexity. - overuse of non‑portable extensions could erode portability if not governed. ## revisit criteria - requirement for global active‑active writes with very low latency and rus‑style elasticity. - dramatic growth in semi‑structured product data where a document store yields major simplicity/cost wins. - need for htap features (heavy analytics on live data) beyond what postgres + replicas can comfortably support. - cost/sla analysis shows a managed document store or distributed sql would materially reduce tco. ## headingSummaries.heading: Context
headingSummaries.summary: We need a standard way to define and provision cloud resources repeatably across environments (dev → prod), enable GitOps/CI-driven deployments, and remain aligned with our agnostic pillar.

headingSummaries.heading: Decision
headingSummaries.summary: Adopt Bicep as our primary IaC for Azure, with a Terraform parity track for critical modules to preserve portability.

infrastructure as code — bicep first, with terraform parity track ## status - proposed → accepted - date: 2025-09-12 - version: 1.0 - supersedes: n/a - superseded by: n/a ## tags infra, iac, devops, automation, portability, azure, governance ## context we need a standard way to define and provision cloud resources repeatably across environments (dev → prod), enable gitops/ci-driven deployments, and remain aligned with our agnostic pillar. primary needs: - fast authoring and first-class azure resource coverage for mvp velocity. - strong validation, preview/diff, and drift detection. - secure ci/cd with oidc (no long-lived cloud secrets). - path to multi-cloud or cloud migration without rewriting everything from scratch. options: bicep (azure’s dsl over arm), terraform (multi-cloud), pulumi (iac in general-purpose languages), raw arm templates, crossplane (kubernetes control-plane managing cloud resources), and azure deployment environments (meta tooling around templates). ## decision adopt bicep as our primary iac for azure, with a terraform parity track for critical modules to preserve portability. - day‑1 / year‑1: ship with bicep for all azure resources (container apps, postgres flexible server, static web apps/front door if used, key vault, log analytics, acr). - maintain a thin terraform mirror for the core runtime (registry, container runtime, database, networking) that compiles in ci (validation only). this ensures we can migrate clouds or orchestration platforms later with lower rewrite risk. - ci/cd: use github actions with oidc to run bicep deployments (and terraform validate/plan for parity) without stored credentials. this choice maximizes azure velocity now while keeping a credible exit/multi-cloud story. ## alternatives considered ### a) terraform (hcl) — multi-cloud first - pros - large ecosystem; mature state management; rich modules. - works across azure/aws/gcp; clearer multi-cloud narrative. - cons - azure resource coverage sometimes lags bicep/arm on day-one features. - managing remote state + rbac adds complexity for a solo founder mvp. - some provider breaking changes and version churn to manage. ### b) pulumi (typescript/python/go) - pros - use real programming languages; strong code reuse/testing. - multi-cloud support comparable to terraform. - cons - smaller ecosystem than terraform; vendor/runtime dependency. - steeper learning curve for infra team used to declarative dsls. ### c) raw arm templates - pros - maximum azure coverage; no translation layer; battle-tested. - cons - verbose/complex json; harder to maintain and review vs bicep. ### d) crossplane (kubernetes-native iac) - pros - gitops with a kubernetes control plane managing cloud resources; composable apis. - cons - requires running/operating a cluster just to provision infra; heavy for mvp. ### e) azure deployment environments / blueprints - pros - standardization and governance for teams at scale. - cons - additional layer; still needs bicep/arm/terraform under the hood. ## portability & agnosticism guarantees - define portable modules with minimal azure‑specific assumptions; document equivalents in terraform for: registry, container runtime, database, networking, secrets, logging. - keep state externalization: data in postgres/object storage; iac describes infra only. - avoid provider‑specific behavior in application code; iac abstraction boundaries stay at resource creation/config only. - maintain a terraform validation ci job (plan/validate) that must pass on each main branch build for core modules. ## ci/cd & security (non-binding outline) - github actions + oidc to assume azure roles at deploy time (no stored secrets). - workflows: deploy-infra-bicep.yml (apply), validate-terraform.yml (plan only initially). - environments: dev, prod with manual approvals; artifacted plans for review. ## consequences - positive - fast azure delivery with bicep authoring and day‑one resource support. - lower complexity than terraform for the mvp while retaining a portability path. - security improvements via oidc and principle of least privilege. - negative / risks - two stacks to maintain conceptually (bicep + terraform parity), albeit the terraform track is validation‑only at first. - true multi-cloud deployment will still require effort to finish terraform modules beyond core. - team must learn two toolchains over time (mitigated by staged adoption). ## revisit criteria - we commit to re-evaluate this adr if: - we plan a multi-cloud expansion or migration off azure. - bicep lacks critical features or lags unacceptably behind new azure services. - our team size grows and we need a shared module ecosystem where terraform adds net value. ## related decisions - adr‑0001: cloud vs on‑prem (azure selected as primary cloud) - adr‑0002: frontend hosting — containerized vs non‑container (containerized chosen) - adr‑0003: runtime for services — containerized vs non‑container (containerized chosen) - adr‑0007: runtime orchestration — aca vs aks (separate adr) ## references - microsoft bicep documentation - terraform azurerm provider documentation - pulumi (azure native provider) documentation - github actions oidc for azure deployments - thoughtworks — adrs and evolutionary architecture

# adr-0048: azure container apps (aca) vs azure kubernetes service (aks) ## status - proposed → accepted - date: 2025-09-12 - version: 1.0 - supersedes: n/a - superseded by: n/a ## tags infra, containers, runtime, orchestration, azure, cost, scaling, portability ## context a decision is needed on the primary container runtime for our services (e.g., n8n, lightweight apis). the previous file name used “acs”, but azure container service (acs) is deprecated. we interpret this decision as azure container apps (aca) vs azure kubernetes service (aks). key drivers: - speed to market for demo → mvp with a solo founder. - operational simplicity with autoscaling and scale-to-zero. - cost efficiency at low-to-medium traffic. - path to scale (multi-region, hpa-style autoscale, advanced networking). - agnostic design (ability to migrate to aks or other clouds later). ## decision adopt azure container apps (aca) as the default runtime for n8n and early microservices for demo → mvp and the initial scale-up phase. we will define clear revisit criteria: if/when we require advanced kubernetes primitives (daemonsets, custom crds/operators, istio-level traffic policies, gpu scheduling at scale, complex service mesh, or per-pod security policies beyond aca’s capabilities), we will author a new adr to transition to aks. ## alternatives considered ### option a — azure container apps (aca) (chosen) - pros - managed serverless containers with scale-to-zero, https ingress, revisions, blue/green. - lower ops burden than aks; no control plane management. - cost efficient at low/variable load; good fit for webhook-driven n8n. - simple integration with log analytics, key vault, container registry. - supports background jobs, event-driven patterns, and dapr if needed. - cons - fewer kubernetes knobs; limited to aca feature set. - advanced networking and gpu options more constrained than aks. - some workloads (high-throughput, fine-grained pod tuning) fit aks better. ### option b — azure kubernetes service (aks) - pros - full kubernetes control: crds, operators, daemonsets, statefulsets, csi drivers. - rich ecosystem (service mesh, gpu scheduling, node pools, taints/tolerations). - best for complex, high-scale, multi-team platforms. - cons - higher operational overhead (cluster lifecycle, node patching, upgrades). - higher baseline cost (control plane + always-on nodes), weaker economics at mvp scale. - longer lead time to production readiness (ingress/waf, certs, monitoring, autoscale configs). ### option c — azure app service (web apps for containers) - pros - managed runtime for always-on web apps; simpler than aks. - good deployment slots, tls, autoscale (not to zero). - cons - not ideal for webhook-heavy bursty workloads; no scale-to-zero. - less flexible for background jobs vs aca. ## consequences - positive - faster time-to-market; minimal ops for the founding team. - lower initial costs (scale-to-zero) while demand is variable. - clear evolutionary path: aca now → aks later if/when needed. - aligns with our agnostic architecture: services packaged as containers are portable to aks, cloud run, ecs/fargate, or on-prem k8s. - negative / risks - potential feature gaps may surface (gpus, advanced networking, sidecars). mitigation: define revisit criteria and test early. - some vendor lock-in at the platform layer. mitigation: containerize everything; keep ingress/protocols standard; avoid aca-only apis in core. ## revisit criteria (trigger a new adr) - need for custom k8s resources/operators or complex service mesh policies. - sustained workloads where always-on nodes are more cost-effective than serverless pricing. - requirement for gpu scheduling at scale or specialized node types. - advanced per-pod security policies/networking not supported by aca. - multi-tenant platform needs (namespaces/quotas) beyond aca’s scope. ## related decisions - adr-0042: cloud vs on-prem (cloud → azure) - adr-0043: frontend hosting choice (swa vs containerized next.js) — pending - adr-0045: database — postgres flexible server — pending - adr-0047 (planned): agnostic architecture principles ## references - azure docs: container apps vs aks capability overviews - azure pricing calculators (aca, aks) - internal cost models for mvp scale

cloud run vs ecs fargate internal cost/perf models for mvp workloads adopt azure container apps (aca) as the default runtime/orchestrator for mvp and scale‑1. # adr-0050: runtime / container orchestration choices ## status - proposed → accepted - date: 2025-09-12 - version: 1.0 - supersedes: n/a - superseded by: n/a ## tags infra, containers, orchestration, runtime, scaling, cost, portability, azure ## context we need a primary orchestration and runtime platform for our containerized services (n8n, api backends, and—by design—our containerized frontend). the platform must: - support http ingress, autosc ale, and scale-to-zero for bursty, webhook-driven workloads. - keep operational overhead low for a solo founder through mvp → early scale. - align with our agnostic pillar so workloads are portable to other clouds or on‑prem if needed. - provide a clear evolution path from mvp to higher-scale / advanced networking scenarios. ## decision adopt azure container apps (aca) as the default runtime/orchestrator for mvp and scale‑1. - use aca revisions for blue/green & canary releases, and built‑in https ingress for public services. - keep all workloads packaged as oci images with standard health probes and http contracts, so they can move to aks, aws ecs/fargate, or gcp cloud run without code changes. - document explicit revisit criteria (below) for when to migrate to aks or alternative orchestrators. ## alternatives considered ### a) azure container apps (aca) — chosen for mvp / scale‑1 - pros - serverless containers with scale-to-zero, https ingress, revisions, blue/green, traffic splitting. - low operational overhead (no control plane to manage) - integrations with log analytics, key vault, acr; supports background jobs. - cons - fewer kubernetes primitives (no crds/daemonsets/stateful sets); gpu and advanced networking are limited. ### b) azure kubernetes service (aks) - pros - full kubernetes control (crds, operators, service mesh, gpu scheduling, custom cni). - strong fit for complex multi-team platforms at high scale. - cons - higher baseline cost and ops burden (cluster lifecycle, node pools, upgrades). - longer time-to-production for a solo founder. ### c) azure app service (web apps for containers) - pros - simple always-on container hosting; deployment slots; managed tls. - cons - no scale-to-zero; less efficient for webhook/bursty workloads. - limited background worker patterns compared to containers with event scale. ### d) gcp cloud run / aws ecs fargate (portability references) - pros - managed/serverless containers with autoscale (cloud run scale-to-zero). - good portability target given our oci image packaging. - cons - different iam, networking, and observability stacks; migration effort required. ### e) self-managed kubernetes (on-prem or cloud vms) - pros - maximum control and portability. - cons - highest operational burden; not aligned with mvp velocity. ## portability & agnosticism guarantees - oci images only; no platform-specific sidecars or proprietary apis in core services. - ingress neutrality: standard http(s) and websocket where needed; avoid aca‑specific assumptions in app code. - state externalized to postgres/object storage via standard drivers. - secrets/config via a provider-agnostic interface (key vault today; swappable later); 12‑factor env usage. - observability via opentelemetry (otlp) so backends are swappable (log analytics ↔ datadog ↔ otel collectors). - maintain a runtime conformance test that can run the containers on aca and on a stock kubernetes (kind/aks) to validate startup, health checks, and graceful shutdown. ## consequences - positive - faster time to market; minimal ops for mvp while retaining a credible path to aks if needed. - cost‑effective for bursty workloads due to scale-to-zero and autoscaling. - consistent deployment story across frontend/backend (all containers). - negative / risks - feature gaps (gpu, advanced networking) could emerge; may require an orchestrator change. - some platform lock-in at the ingress/observability layer (mitigated by agnostic contracts). ## revisit criteria (trigger a new adr) - need for custom k8s primitives (crds/operators), daemonsets, or statefulsets. - requirement for gpu scheduling at scale, or per‑pod security/networking policies exceeding aca’s features. - sustained high, predictable load where always-on nodes are more cost‑efficient than serverless. - multi‑tenant isolation and quota mechanisms beyond what aca supports. - complex service mesh/traffic policies (mtls, canary at mesh layer) not achievable in aca. ## related decisions - adr‑0001: cloud vs on‑prem (azure chosen) - adr‑0002: frontend hosting — containerized vs non‑container (containerized chosen) - adr‑0003: runtime for services — containerized vs non‑container (containerized chosen) - adr‑0004: database — postgresql - adr‑0005: iac — bicep with terraform parity ## references - azure docs on container apps features (revisions, traffic splitting, autoscale) - comparisons: aca vs aks; cloud run vs ecs fargate - internal cost/perf models for mvp workloads

service communication patterns — hybrid (pub/sub + orchestration + graphql bff) ## status - proposed → accepted - date: 2025-09-12 - version: 1.0 - supersedes: n/a - superseded by: n/a ## tags architecture, services, communication, events, orchestration, graphql, rest, portability, observability ## context we must choose how services communicate across the platform. the solution should: - support long-running, multi-step flows (e.g., search → curate → approve → purchase) that involve ai/n8n integrations and compensations. - allow the frontend to assemble data from multiple backends efficiently. - remain vendor-agnostic and portable, with standard protocols and contracts. - scale from mvp to early growth without a major rewrite, and keep reliability high (retries, idempotency). ## decision adopt a hybrid communication model: 1) event-driven (pub/sub) for domain events and async processing use a message bus for decoupled workflows and fan-out (e.g., search.completed, feedback.recorded, click.tracked). guarantees: at-least-once delivery, idempotent consumers, dead-letter queues, and outbox pattern from the oltp db. 2) orchestrated workflows for long-running business processes use n8n as the orchestrator for multi-step flows with retries/compensations (e.g., approval to purchase). orchestrator communicates with services via http/webhooks and publishes/consumes events. revisit a durable engine (temporal/durable functions) if complexity/volume warrants it. 3) graphql bff (backend-for-frontend) for the ui and business-facing apis the frontend calls a single graphql endpoint which aggregates data from internal services (via rest or grpc later). this reduces chatty calls from the ui and centralises access control and caching/persisted queries. keep schema domain-driven and versioned. 4) rest/json at the edges and between services initially use simple http/rest between services to start (clear, portable). consider grpc for internal high-throughput paths later; keep graphql resolvers talking to rest/grpc adapters. deferred: real-time push (sse/websockets) is not required now; leave as a future addition when live updates become a product need. ## alternatives considered - all rest: simple but tightly coupled; harder to scale and evolve; no native async. - all grpc: high performance internally but browser-unfriendly and adds infra overhead now. - event-only (choreography): maximum decoupling but complex to coordinate compensations; harder observability. - graphql-only: great for ui aggregation but insufficient for async, long-running flows and platform integrations. ## portability & agnosticism guarantees - contracts: openapi for rest and json schema/cloudevents for events; graphql schema versioned with deprecation policy. - outbox pattern: domain events written to postgres outbox and relayed to the bus to avoid lost messages. - idempotency: all side-effecting rest endpoints accept an idempotency-key; consumers dedupe by message id. - observability: opentelemetry traces/metrics/logs across rest, graphql, and events; propagate traceid in headers/envelopes. - provider neutrality: message bus via an abstraction (azure service bus initially; swappable to sqs/sns, pub/sub, rabbit/kafka). orchestrator uses http/contracts, not vendor sdks. ## consequences - positive - decoupled services with resilient async processing; clear orchestration for complex flows. - frontend benefits from a single graphql endpoint (fewer round trips; cleaner auth/policy). - portable protocols and artifacts; easier to migrate runtimes/clouds. - negative / risks - added complexity vs a pure rest approach (bus + orchestrator + graphql gateway). - requires careful schema governance (events + graphql) and idempotency discipline. - gateway (graphql bff) can become a bottleneck if not scaled/observed properly. ## revisit criteria - throughput/latency pressure between services → consider grpc for internal rpc. - workflow complexity/volume exceeds n8n comfort → evaluate temporal/durable functions. - ui composition strains graphql or needs edge execution → evaluate persisted queries, cdn caching, or edge gateways. - operational overhead of bus/orchestrator outweighs benefits for a prolonged period → simplify to rest-first for affected domains. ## related decisions - adr‑0002: frontend hosting — containerized vs non‑container (containerized chosen) - adr‑0003: runtime for services — containerized vs non‑container (containerized chosen) - adr‑0004: database — postgresql - adr‑0005: iac — bicep first with terraform parity - adr‑0009: runtime / container orchestration — aca chosen for mvp/scale‑1 ## references - cloudevents specification - opentelemetry specs for traces/metrics/logs - graphql best practices (schema versioning, persisted queries) - outbox pattern and idempotency keys in distributed systems

github actions (oidc) + container revisions ## status - proposed → accepted - date: 2025-09-12 - version: 1.0 - supersedes: n/a - superseded by: n/a ## tags cicd, devops, containers, security, supply-chain, rollback, portability ## context we need a standard, repeatable pipeline to build, test, secure, and deploy services (apis, n8n, and the containerized frontend). the pipeline must: - produce a single deployable artifact (oci image) per service. - support canary/blue‑green rollouts and instant rollback. - use least‑privilege, secretless cloud auth (oidc) from ci. - provide supply‑chain integrity (image signing, sbom, vulnerability scan). - remain vendor‑agnostic so we can move to other clouds/registries/runtimes. ## decision adopt github actions for ci/cd with openid connect (oidc) to assume cloud roles, building versioned oci images and deploying via container revisions (e.g., aca revisions / equivalent on other runtimes). the key points: - artifact: each service builds a versioned oci image (app:vx.y.z+gitsha) pushed to a registry (acr today; any oci registry later). - quality gates: lint + unit/integration tests; container vulnerability scan; generate sbom; sign images. - deployment strategy: use revisions with traffic splitting for canary/blue‑green; promote to 100% on health; retain n‑1 revision for instant rollback. - environments: dev (auto on main), staging (manual approval), prod (manual approval + change record). - auth: ci uses oidc to get short‑lived cloud tokens; no long‑lived credentials in repo. - observability gates: post‑deploy smoke test; watch key slos (error rate, p95 latency) before promotion. this pipeline is portable: it emits standard oci images, signs them, and relies on revision‑based rollout wherever available (aca, cloud run, ecs, aks with rollout controller). ## alternatives considered ### a) azure devops pipelines pros: deep azure integration; approvals/gates; enterprise features. cons: extra platform to run; less aligned with our github‑first workflow. ### b) gitlab ci/cd pros: strong built‑in registry, security scanning, and approvals. cons: requires gitlab hosting or migration; we are already on github. ### c) jenkins / self‑hosted runners only pros: full control; can run anywhere. cons: high operational overhead; security hardening required; not ideal for solo founder. ### d) argocd / flux (gitops) pros: declarative pull‑based deploy; great for k8s. cons: adds cluster‑level components; heavier than needed for aca‑first mvp; revisit for aks. ## portability & agnosticism guarantees - standard artifacts: oci images published to open container initiative‑compliant registries; no proprietary image formats. - signing & sbom: use sigstore/cosign for image signing and spdx/cyclonedx sboms so attestation travels with the artifact across clouds. - secretless ci: oidc‑based federation to assume cloud roles (azure today; aws/gcp analogues later). - runtime‑neutral rollout: canary/blue‑green via revision or rollout controller; do not hardcode aca‑specific apis in app code. - contracts: health checks (/healthz), readiness probes, and smoke tests are runtime‑agnostic. ## release process (non‑binding outline) 1. build: lint, test, build image; stamp with vx.y.z+sha. 2. secure: sbom generation; vulnerability scan; sign image. 3. publish: push to registry; annotate with labels (commit, build time, slsa level). 4. deploy: create new revision with 0–10% traffic; run smoke tests and watch slos. 5. promote: gradually shift to 100% if healthy; keep previous revision warm for fast rollback. 6. rollback: re-point traffic to previous revision on failure; open incident and capture logs/traces. ## consequences - positive - strong security posture (secretless auth, signed images, sboms). - reproducible, portable deployments across clouds/runtimes. - safer releases via canary/blue‑green and instant rollback. - negative / risks - extra ci minutes for scans/signing; minor cost/time overhead. - registry and signing infrastructure need governance (keyless workflows, policy enforcement). - more moving parts than a simple git push to paas. ## revisit criteria - if we adopt aks + gitops, consider moving to argocd/flux for pull‑based deploys while keeping github actions for build/sign. - if ci minutes or limits become a bottleneck, evaluate self‑hosted runners or alternative ci providers. - if regulatory requirements demand different signing/attestation standards, update the pipeline accordingly. ## related decisions - adr‑0002: frontend hosting — containerized vs non‑container (containerized chosen) - adr‑0003: runtime for services — containerized vs non‑container (containerized chosen) - adr‑0005: iac — bicep first with terraform parity - adr‑0009: runtime / container orchestration — aca for mvp/scale‑1 - adr‑0010: service communication patterns — hybrid (pub/sub + orchestration + graphql bff) ## references - github actions oidc for cloud providers - sigstore cosign & keyless signing - spdx / cyclonedx sbom standards - slsa framework (supply chain levels) - azure container apps revisions & traffic splitting

workspaces and clear boundaries ## status - proposed → accepted - date: 2025-09-12 - version: 1.0 - supersedes: n/a - superseded by: n/a ## tags repo, packaging, monorepo, workspaces, versioning, ci, governance, portability ## current state note (2026-06-04) the hybrid strategy described here has advanced to published package polyrepos for reusable/public @plasius/ functionality. for the active plasius-ltd-site repository boundary, see adr 0085: this repo now owns only the frontend and backend application workspaces plus docs, infra, and specs. new reusable package implementation work should happen in the owning package repository unless a local workspace is intentionally reintroduced. ## context we must choose how to organise source code for the frontend, backend services, shared libraries (types, domain models), infrastructure definitions, and tests. the choice impacts developer velocity, code reuse, consistency, ci/cd complexity, and our pillar of being agnostic and portable. requirements: - single‑founder → small team ramp: maximise dx and speed with minimal repo sprawl. - shared domain contracts (types/schemas) across frontend, services, and n8n nodes. - reproducible builds, atomic changes across components, and straightforward code ownership. - ability to extract components later if scaling/org boundaries require it. ## decision adopt a hybrid strategy: a private monorepo for core apps/services and separate polyrepos for oss packages for the first 12–18 months. - private monorepo holds core services, apps, infra, and proprietary packages like @plasius/core-ranking, @plasius/memory, and @plasius/personalisation. - use workspaces (pnpm or npm/yarn) within the private monorepo for shared packages: @plasius/domain, @plasius/contracts, @plasius/utils, @plasius/ui. - add a light build/orchestration tool (e.g., turborepo or nx) for incremental builds, caching, and task pipelines. - enforce module boundaries via lints (no circular deps, no cross‑layer imports except through public apis). - versioning strategy: start with single version stream (monorepo at vx.y.z) for simplicity; revisit independent versions if needed. - ci optimisations: cache builds/test results, affected‑only pipelines, and per‑package publishing when relevant. - clear ownership files (codeowners) per package/app. - oss repos include: - @plasius/contracts - @plasius/adapters- - @plasius/utils - @plasius/entity-manager this gives fast iteration and shared contracts without scatter. we will revisit if team size, compliance, or delivery models push us to split further. ## alternatives considered ### a) polyrepo (multiple repos per service/package) - pros - natural isolation; independent lifecycles and permissions. - mirrors org structures at scale. cons - coordination overhead for shared contracts; cross‑repo changes are slower. - ci setup per repo; duplicated tooling/config. ### b) hybrid (monorepo for shared libs + critical apps, separate repos for infra or edge services) - pros - balance between speed and isolation; can keep infra/iac independent if governance demands. - cons - still adds complexity in release management and dependency updates. ### c) giant monolith (single app) - pros - simplest to begin; zero package boundaries. - cons - limits portability and growth; hard to enforce contracts and testing surfaces. ## portability & agnosticism guarantees - contracts as packages: domain models and api schemas live in @plasius/contracts. services import contracts from this package only; no vendor sdks in shared code. - adapter boundaries: vendor‑specific code goes in @plasius/adapters/; core logic only depends on ports/interfaces. - replaceable build runner: turborepo/nx is tooling only; packages remain standard node packages. - publishable artifacts: shared packages can be published to a registry (private npm/gh‑packages) to support extraction to polyrepo later. ## repo layout (illustrative) `text / (repo) apps/ web/ # frontend (containerized) api-gateway/ # graphql bff svc-search/ # service(s) behind the bff svc-affiliate/ # link/attribution service svc-feedback/ # feedback ingestion packages/ domain/ # domain entities, value objects (@plasius/domain) contracts/ # openapi/graphql schemas, json schemas (@plasius/contracts - oss repo) utils/ # shared helpers (@plasius/utils - oss repo) ui/ # design system components (@plasius/ui) adapters/ # external vendor adapters (awin, cj, amazon, ebay, llm) (@plasius/adapters/ - oss repos) entity-manager/ # entity management library (@plasius/entity-manager - oss repo) workflows/ # n8n json exports (versioned) infra/ # iac (bicep + tf parity) tools/ # scripts, codegen ` ## versioning & releases - start with a single semantic version for the monorepo (v0.x` during mvp), tag on the main branch. - use conventional commits and auto‑changelog generation. - when publishing internal packages (if needed), use workspace protocol and version synchronously; switch to independent package versions only if justified. ## ci/cd - pipeline stages: lint → test → build → package (affected only) with caching. - on merge to main: build all affected apps/services; publish images; update revisions. - optionally publish internal packages to github packages when version bumps are detected. ## consequences - positive - faster cross‑cutting changes (schema + implementations) in a single pr. - single source of truth for contracts and ui components; fewer drift issues. - simpler onboarding and tooling for a small team; strong dx. - negative / risks - repo size and ci times can grow; needs caching and affected‑only builds. - requires discipline to enforce boundaries; without it, coupling can creep in. - some enterprise workflows expect polyrepo separation (can be handled later). ## revisit criteria - team grows beyond 8–12 engineers and boundaries become contentious. - compliance or partner requirements demand separate repos (e.g., payment service isolation). - ci times become a bottleneck despite caching and affected‑only builds. - oss packages will always remain polyrepo, but additional extraction may occur as the team scales. ## related decisions - adr‑0002: frontend hosting — containerized vs non‑container (containerized chosen) - adr‑0003: runtime for services — containerized vs non‑container shopify) - turborepo / nx documentation - conventional commits & semantic release

headingSummaries.heading: Context

headingSummaries.summary: Positive

headingSummaries.heading: Revisit Criteria
headingSummaries.summary: If maintenance/support load exceeds capacity → reconsider scope of OSS. If community traction is low → consolidate OSS packages or reduce footprint. If licensing strategy needs to change for commercial partnerships → revisit dual-licensing or source-available.

architecture adopt a selective open-source strategy: # adr-0054: open source strategy — selective oss for ecosystem growth ## status - proposed → accepted - date: 2025-09-12 - version: 1.0 - supersedes: n/a - superseded by: n/a ## tags open-source, strategy, licensing, governance, plasius, ecosystem ## context to drive adoption, credibility, and ecosystem growth, we must decide what parts of the platform to open source and how. our guiding principle: share the building blocks, keep the engine proprietary. goals: - build trust and visibility in the developer and partner community. - encourage contributions to adapters and shared utilities. - create a standard set of contracts and entity definitions so partners can integrate directly. - retain proprietary advantage in personalisation, ranking, and business analytics. ## decision adopt a selective open-source strategy: - oss packages (polyrepo under @plasius): - @plasius/contracts — api schemas, json schemas, graphql definitions. - @plasius/adapters- — vendor-specific search/affiliate adapters (amazon, ebay, etsy, cj, awin, etc.). - @plasius/utils — shared helpers (logging, error wrappers, date/time, etc.). - @plasius/entity-manager — consistent entity definition/validation across packages. - proprietary (private monorepo): - core ranking/personalisation logic. - feedback memory system (user preferences). - business dashboards and analytics. - orchestration flows and ai integration logic. licensing: - apache-2.0 for all oss packages (permissive, encourages adoption). - proprietary packages under plasius ip; closed source. repos: - each oss package lives in its own github repo under the plasius organisation. - private monorepo (plasius/intuitive-purchasing) hosts core services, infra, apps. ## alternatives considered - open everything: faster adoption, but risks losing proprietary advantage and monetisation path. - keep all closed: protects ip, but slows ecosystem growth and partner integrations. - source-available (busl): middle ground, but reduces community adoption vs permissive licensing. ## governance & contribution - each oss repo includes: license, readme, contributing.md, codeofconduct.md, security.md. - contribution model: dco sign-offs or cla assistant for external prs. - semantic versioning with changelogs. - triage cadence: weekly issue/pr review; security advisories as needed. - clear boundary between oss (building blocks) and proprietary (engine). ## consequences - positive - ecosystem growth via contributions and partner integration. - oss packages become trust anchors (contracts, adapters, utils). - developer visibility and potential contributor pipeline. - reinforces our trust pillar by being transparent and open with core building blocks. - negative / risks - extra maintenance and governance overhead for oss repos. - coordination overhead between oss package versions and internal monorepo. - risk of copycats using oss to replicate parts of the platform (mitigated by keeping core proprietary). ## revisit criteria - if maintenance/support load exceeds capacity → reconsider scope of oss. - if community traction is low → consolidate oss packages or reduce footprint. - if licensing strategy needs to change for commercial partnerships → revisit dual-licensing or source-available. ## related decisions - adr-0053: package strategy — hybrid (private monorepo + oss polyrepo under @plasius/\) - adr-0046: iac — bicep first with terraform parity - adr-0052: service deployment pipeline — github actions + revisions ## adrs.summary: Adopt the existing capability-rule model as the only MCP capability control plane, with canonical identifiers derived from the rule tuple rather than a new capability resource.
adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0055-mcp-capability-actions-over-scoped-capability-rules.md mcp capability actions over scoped capability rules accepted 2026-04-24 context decision consequences related decisions references context feature #147 and story #151 extend the mcp admin registry from discovery-only feature-flag actions into capability actions. decision adopt the existing capability-rule model as the only mcp capability control plane, with canonical identifiers derived from the rule tuple rather than a new capability resource. consequences positive: the mcp contract now matches adr 0025 and the backend routes that already exist, agents get stable, human-readable capability identifiers without being forced to understand storage ids up front, payload-bearing and windowed capability rules stay l... related decisions adr 0025: user-scoped capabilities as the single control surface (with target routing) adr 0037: mcp admin discovery registry over existing admin routes adr 0038: mcp admin discovery safety, authorization, and audit verification references docs/api/mcp-admin-discovery.md docs/design/mcp-interface-design.md github feature #147, story #151, task #152, task #153 adopt the existing capability-rule model as the only mcp capability control plane, with canonical identifiers derived from the rule tuple rather than a new capability resource. # adr 0055: mcp capability actions over scoped capability rules - status: accepted - date: 2026-04-24 ## context feature #147 and story #151 extend the mcp admin registry from discovery-only feature-flag actions into capability actions. the backend already has one capability source of truth: - mutable capability rules stored through post|delete /api/ops/capability-rules, - effective capability reads returned by get /api/users/me/capabilities/{service}, - verification and history emitted into the shared admin audit stream under family=admin.capability-rule.update. the remaining gap was not storage or a missing route. it was contract shape. the mcp design notes still described a generic /capabilities/{capabilitykey} resource, which risks implying a second capability model that conflicts with adr 0025. the mcp contract also needed a stable way to describe payload-bearing and windowed rules without forcing agents to reason about backend table entity internals. ## decision adopt the existing capability-rule model as the only mcp capability control plane, with canonical identifiers derived from the rule tuple rather than a new capability resource. 1. use a two-level mcp identifier model: - effective capability key: service=service;capability=capability - mutable rule key: service=service;capability=capability;scope=scope;subject=subject-or- 2. keep effective reads on get /api/users/me/capabilities/{service}. - getcapability resolves one effective capability by service plus capability. - the response surfaces the existing payload, window, source rule metadata, and transition metadata instead of inventing a second record type. 3. keep assignments and updates on post /api/ops/capability-rules. - assigncapability and updatecapability are defined by service/capability/scope/subject. - a discovered backend ruleid may be carried as an optimization or verification hint, but it is not the canonical mcp identifier. 4. keep deletes on delete /api/ops/capability-rules/{id} behind destructive confirmation. - unassigncapability accepts the canonical rule tuple plus the destructive confirmation token. - the adapter resolves that tuple to the backing ruleid before calling the delete route. 5. surface payload-bearing and windowed rules without translation. - payload kind, target, params, and schema version remain aligned with the backend capability payload contract, - time windows remain aligned with the backend startsat/endsat model, - agents must preserve unknown payload params rather than normalizing them away. 6. reuse the shared admin audit plane for verification and rollback evidence. - capability mutations verify through get /api/ops/audit/events?family=admin.capability-rule.update, - operator rollback stays anchored to mcp.admin.liveops-controls.enabled plus the existing capability-rule admin routes; no mcp-specific history store or rollback-only resource is introduced. ## consequences - positive: - the mcp contract now matches adr 0025 and the backend routes that already exist, - agents get stable, human-readable capability identifiers without being forced to understand storage ids up front, - payload-bearing and windowed capability rules stay lossless across discovery, mutation, and verification, - audit verification and rollback continue to reuse the shared admin control plane. - negative: - destructive capability deletes still require a tuple-to-ruleid lookup before calling the existing delete route, - the contract has to describe both canonical tuple identifiers and the resolved backend ruleid, - capability verification remains audit-query driven instead of a dedicated getcapabilityhistory tool in 2026-04-09.v1. ## related decisions - adr 0025: user-scoped capabilities as the single control surface (with target routing) - adr 0037: mcp admin discovery registry over existing admin routes - adr 0038: mcp admin discovery safety, authorization, and audit verification ## references - docs/api/mcp-admin-discovery.md - docs/design/mcp-interface-design.md -
