status: accepted - date: 2026-04-24 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context feature #154 introduces analytics and user-aggregation reads for the mcp admin surface. the current backend already exposes: - get /api/ops/analytics/report for blob-backed operational analytics, - get /api/ops/analytics/alert-policies, - get /api/ops/analytics/advisories. the discovery registry already advertises analytics actions, but the analytics descriptors are still too loose. they imply a more generic query model than the backend actually supports and do not document which metrics, dimensions, presets, or parameters are safe for mcp callers. story #155 requires a bounded analytics contract before the analytics family can be considered implementation-ready under mcp.admin.analytics.enabled. ## decision 1. keep the analytics mcp family behind the dedicated rollout flag mcp.admin.analytics.enabled, while the existing parent exposure gate mcp.admin.production-readiness.enabled continues to govern whether the public mcp manifest and discovery routes are exposed at all. 2. reuse the existing admin analytics routes as the only v1 execution surfaces: - get /api/ops/analytics/report for report-backed analytics queries, - get /api/ops/analytics/alert-policies and get /api/ops/analytics/advisories only for the curated notificationshealth preset. 3. curate the v1 analytics metric whitelist to: - totalevents - errorevents - fatalevents - uniqueidentities - uniqueiphashes - thresholdtriggercount 4. curate the v1 analytics dimension whitelist to: - timeline - source - component - action - errorfingerprint 5. constrain the supported metric and dimension matrix to the current report sections: - totalevents -> timeline, source, component, action - errorevents -> timeline, errorfingerprint - fatalevents -> timeline, errorfingerprint - uniqueidentities -> timeline - uniqueiphashes -> timeline - thresholdtriggercount -> errorfingerprint 6. curate the preset whitelist to: - adminoverview - recenterrors - notificationshealth 7. limit the mcp analytics parameter envelope to: - lookbackhours - bucketminutes - topn - thresholdcount - thresholdwindowminutes 8. keep maxblobsscan backend-controlled. mcp callers must not tune blob-scan breadth directly because that would increase load and weaken the backend’s operational guardrails. 9. reuse the existing admin analytics audit family family=admin.analytics.query for analytics read verification and continue returning the existing bounded storage-unavailable responses from the backing admin routes. 10. treat the schema tightening for analytics descriptors as a discovery contract revision and bump the discovery contract version to 2026-04-24.v2. ## consequences ### positive - mcp analytics queries now describe the real backend surfaces instead of a vague future analytics engine. - the analytics whitelist is explicit and testable in both code and docs. - operators retain rollback through mcp.admin.analytics.enabled or, at a higher level, mcp.admin.production-readiness.enabled. - the contract keeps privacy and performance boundaries visible before the analytics family is enabled publicly. ### negative - the analytics schema is stricter than the earlier placeholder-style v1 descriptor, so the discovery contract version must advance. - notificationshealth is a composed preset over two existing admin routes, which is more operationally coupled than the pure report-backed presets. - user aggregation remains separate follow-on work under story #158; this adr does not solve the grouped-user summary contract. ## related decisions - adr 0037: mcp admin discovery registry over existing admin routes - adr 0038: mcp admin discovery safety, authorization, and audit verification ## references - docs/api/mcp-admin-discovery.md - docs/how-to-guides/mcp-admin-rollout-controls.md - package through the n... # adr 0057: public-safe backend api and mcp package extraction ## status accepted ## context task #259 reviews whether backend api and mcp code can move from the private backend into public packages without exposing private data or weakening site security. the backend currently mixes three categories of code: - public-safe contract metadata, such as mcp action names, response shapes, route mappings, and rollout flag identifiers - runtime enforcement code, such as auth, authorization, rate limiting, rollout evaluation, and audit emission - private operational code, such as data clients, admin mutations, oauth session handling, ai/media processing, and analytics/user data access ## decision use @plasius/mcp-admin-contracts as the first extracted package in its own standalone repository (plasius-ltd/mcp-admin-contracts) and move only mcp discovery contract metadata and pure response builders into it. the site consumes this package through the npm package name, not as a local workspace reference. the backend keeps: - http route registration and azure functions bindings - withadminauth, full-session authorization, and concealed admin responses - withmcpadminrollout and feature-flag evaluation - rate limiting and mcp header enforcement - audit writing and operational logging - table/blob clients, oauth/session handling, ai/media execution, analytics reads, user/profile reads, and every mutation implementation the feature continues to use the existing runtime rollout controls: - mcp.admin.production-readiness.enabled - mcp.admin.foundation.enabled no new public runtime endpoint is introduced by the package extraction. ## architectural review | surface | extraction stance | rationale | | --- | --- | --- | | mcp manifest, action descriptors, schema shape, context shape, action-family grouping, and flag identifiers | move now to @plasius/mcp-admin-contracts | static contract metadata and pure builders are safe to publish when they contain no data clients, secrets, session logic, or live payloads. | | mcp route handlers (/api/mcp/actions, /api/mcp/schema, /api/mcp/context) | keep private | they enforce admin auth, rollout, rate limits, audit emission, and http response semantics. | | mcp rollout evaluators | keep private | they read feature flags from private storage and include fail-closed operational policy. | | mcp audit writer | keep private | it writes tamper-evident admin audit events and must not expose internal audit storage details. | | generic middleware already in @plasius/api | already public-safe | shared middleware primitives are reusable when they remain generic and caller-supplied policy stays local. | | admin feature-flag, capability, destructive-confirmation, audit, analytics, moderation, notification, translation, and users apis | keep private | they expose privileged control-plane behavior or private operational data. public packages may contain future dto/schema contracts only. | | oauth, refresh-token, session, bootstrap, linked-identity, mfa, profile, settings, avatar, video, ai, and analytics ingestion apis | keep private | these surfaces handle identity, user data, credentials, media, ai provider access, or private telemetry. | | public docs/build-info, public legal well-known files, i18n language reads, and security pgp metadata | candidate for later contract package only | route contracts can be public, but handlers and deployment/runtime metadata stay private. | | typespec/openapi generated artifacts | candidate for later sanitized contract package | generated artifacts must be reviewed for private path, admin route, and schema leakage before publishing. | ## security rules - public packages must not import @azure/functions, storage clients, table clients, auth/session modules, audit writers, or backend runtime modules. - public packages must not read environment variables or contain secrets, connection strings, local settings, production payloads, or user records. - public mcp contracts may describe route paths and allowed action names, but they must not execute those actions. - runtime consumers must enforce auth, authorization, rollout gates, rate limits, audit emission, and input validation outside the package. - future public api contract packages must publish dto/schema metadata only and must include a package check equivalent to pack:check. ## consequences - the mcp discovery contract becomes reusable and testable outside the private backend. - publishing the package does not expose internal data because the extracted code has no data access capability. - the backend remains the only place where privileged operations are authorized, audited, and executed. - wider api extraction should proceed as separate tickets after each candidate surface has a privacy review and sanitized contract shape.

status: accepted - date: 2026-05-13 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context planned production deploys for plasius-ltd-site use manual github actions deployment through cd.yml and deploy-aca-warm.sh. before this change, every deployment path could trigger image builds in the cd workflow even when those images were already compiled for the same commit. this increased deployment duration and required duplicate compute work when images already existed in acr. ## decision 1. introduce a rollout gate for runtime optimization: - source of truth feature flag: ops.cicd.runtime-optimization.enabled (repository variable alias opscicdruntimeoptimizationfeatureflag) - break-glass override: opscicdruntimeoptimizationenabled - resolution lives in tools/azure/deploy-aca-warm-lib.sh via resolveruntimeoptimizationenabled(). 2. add a dedicated ci publish step that builds and tags backend/frontend aca images on push to main as: - backend: plasius-ltd-site-backend:deploy-commit-sha - frontend: plasius-ltd-site-frontend:deploy-commit-sha 3. add a cd pre-deploy publish step that uses the same runtime gate and writes build-artifacts/deploy-image-refs.json for deploy traceability. 4. keep deployment script behavior feature-gated: - when optimization is enabled, deployment reuses existing tag-pinned images and skips source rebuild. - when optimization is disabled or not available, deployment falls back to source build behavior with existing safeguards. 5. preserve emergency control: - forceimagerebuild=true in cd input always forces source rebuild paths even when optimization is enabled. ## alternatives considered - always rebuild images in cd: - predictable but slower and duplicate work. - build outside cd on a separate pipeline and never build in cd: - reduces deploy time but increases coupling to ci timing and failure recovery paths. - this approach keeps both paths: optimized reuse by default where enabled, with explicit break-glass fallback to source rebuild. ## consequences ### positive - deployment window is reduced when images are already published for the target commit. - recovery path remains available (forceimagerebuild=true) for unusual image drift or artifact corruption. - governance and release evidence gain a consistent publish path through tools/azure/publish-deploy-artifacts.sh. ### negative - runtime optimization is gated by repository variables and manual override discipline. - ci now requires oidc/azure access to publish acr artifacts when the flag is enabled. - deployments are still fully capable without this flag by retaining source build behavior. ## related decisions - status: proposed - date: 2026-05-14 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the isekai initiative already defines mcc law, identity truth, guild structures, influence systems, and world-event authority. the new player system needs to unify player-facing guidance, audio and visual feedback, preference learning, and focused interaction without replacing those underlying authorities. if the player system becomes an omniscient or disconnected ui shell, it will conflict with existing world law and create an out-of-world cheat layer. ## decision 1. model the player system as a diegetic orchestration context over authoritative world state rather than as an omniscient ui shell. 2. keep invocation state, overlay composition, notification priority, tutorial state, player-model summaries, and command preflight inside the player system boundary. 3. keep identity, missions, guild quests, event logs, mcc guidance, tutorials, and stores as distinct child modules under one system shell. 4. treat the party system as a sibling overlay surface, not as a player system child module. 5. treat item crafting, spell crafting, and dungeon crafting as distinct authoritative external systems that may share player system presentation conventions without moving authority into the player system. 6. require all system outputs to remain bounded by player-observable truth, player tier, mcc feasibility, guild authority, institutional authority, and chaos/resource rules. 7. support ambient speech plus focused 3d system surfaces, with reduced combat-safe presentation. 8. before stage 3 social-form lock, the player system is the only guaranteed conversational interface available to the player. 9. make player preference learning an explicit system responsibility rather than scattering it ad hoc across child modules. ## alternatives considered - separate non-diegetic menus for each subsystem: - simpler in isolation but fragments the player experience and weakens the "system" fantasy. - omniscient all-knowing assistant: - more convenient but incompatible with identity truth, guild authority, and progression fairness. - hard-scripted tutorial shell with no adaptive learning: - easier to build, but it fails the long-term mission and guidance goal. ## consequences ### positive - the player system can feel like one coherent presence while still respecting existing authority boundaries. - later implementation can share one invocation and focus model across many child systems. - preference-driven missions, tutorials, and mcc guidance gain a common orchestration contract. - external crafting systems can stay authoritative while still feeling diegetically consistent to the player. ### negative - the system shell becomes a cross-cutting dependency that must integrate with many world subsystems. - strong authority boundaries reduce opportunities for shortcut implementations. - service-boundary discipline is required to stop system convenience from leaking into domain ownership. ## related decisions - tdr-0027 player system runtime orchestration - tdr-0018 gs authority and world event consolidation

status: proposed - date: 2026-05-14 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the player system must start by guiding a newly awakened player, then transition into more tailored missions once it understands their preferred path. static quest scripting alone will not satisfy that goal, but unrestricted adaptive rewards would violate progression fairness. ## decision 1. use a confidence-scored player model to adapt system missions over time. 2. keep bootstrap missions conservative until enough signal exists to tailor behavior. 3. distinguish system missions from guild quests and other external contract surfaces. 4. limit rewards to bounded accelerants aligned with player readiness rather than direct power skips. 5. let mission acceptance, refusal, and abandonment feed the player model. ## alternatives considered - status: proposed - date: 2026-05-15 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the player system needs recent recall for the player, achievement progression that can be explained from first principles, and observed-event pipelines that can still feed gossip and social consequence. the earlier log design established one canonical observed-event basis for player recall and gossip export, but it did not define where the high-volume event data should live, how it should be processed, or how to keep storage privacy-safe. writing that event history into the operational database would increase write volume, increase query pressure, and blur the line between transactional authority data and analytical or recall-oriented event history. the user-facing event log and achievement section is also rollout-sensitive and discoverable. it therefore needs both backend rollback control and a user-visible access decision. ## decision 1. use one canonical observed-event basis for player recall, achievement projection, and gossip export. 2. persist player-observable events as json in blob-backed storage rather than in the operational database. 3. organize the event pipeline as a small data lake: - raw append-only event batches - normalized observed-event batches - curated per-player event log and achievement read models 4. use timer-triggered azure functions to validate, deduplicate, compact, rank, and project raw batches into curated player-facing datasets. 5. use @plasius/schema to validate ingress envelopes and to serialize storage-safe event records. no sensitive data beyond playerid may be written to raw, normalized, or curated storage. 6. exclude hidden server-only truths from player recall, player-visible achievement evidence, and player-origin gossip surfaces. 7. roll out the end-user section behind feature flag isekai.player-system.events-achievements.enabled and capability player-system.events-achievements.view. ## alternatives considered - separate isolated systems for logs, achievements, and gossip: - easier to specialize, but risks divergent event typing and inconsistent player explanations. - operational database tables for event logs and achievement projections: - familiar query model, but higher write amplification and more pressure on transactional infrastructure. - debug-first event history exposed directly to players: - comprehensive, but non-diegetic, noisy, and harder to keep privacy-safe. - gossip without player logs or achievements: - simpler, but weakens recall, explanation, and player-facing progression. ## consequences ### positive - observed-event consistency improves across player-facing and world-facing features. - event history moves away from the operational database and toward cheaper, batch-friendly blob storage. - achievements gain deterministic evidence from the same canonical event basis used for recall and gossip. - the player system gains better support for recommendation, tutorial replay, and social consequence summaries. ### negative - canonical event typing, storage hygiene, and filtering quality become more important. - batch latency must be managed so the player-facing event log and achievement section stays fresh enough for normal use. - blob checkpointing and reprocessing flows become a new operational concern. ## related decisions - tdr-0031 event log and achievement projection from a blob-backed observed-event lake - adr-0005 structured gossip topics as the output boundary (@plasius/ai-game)

status: proposed - date: 2026-05-14 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the player system introduces pp, esp, tis, and dis as separate point ledgers with different world meanings. the new design also changes existing evolution doctrine by allowing a paid return-to-slime choice during the second-stage proto-social window, while keeping later race choice permanent. the older influence wording also framed tis and dis as scores, which is no longer the preferred player-facing or institutional model. ## decision 1. keep pp, esp, tis, and dis as separate ledgers with separate earning logic, visible income/outgoing history, and separate spend authorities. 2. treat pp as the only ledger permitted to govern personal presentation changes, mcc composition adjustment, death loss, mcc repair obligations, and the proto-social return-to-slime choice. 3. permit the return-to-slime path only before social-form lock and only as an explicit system-mediated pp action. 4. preserve the existing permanent race lock after the player evolves beyond the proto-social second-stage window. 5. keep tis and dis aligned to existing civic/cosmic banding rules instead of collapsing them into one store currency. 6. represent tis and dis as points ledgers rather than score counters so civic and divine spending commitments can be surfaced transparently to players. ## alternatives considered - single unified store currency: - simpler to explain, but destroys authority boundaries and world flavor. - no devolution path after first evolution: - cleaner with earlier doctrine, but less supportive of correcting early-path mismatch. - free respec-style devolution: - more flexible, but too permissive for the world model. ## consequences ### positive - each points family keeps a clear world meaning. - the proto-social devolution window gives players one corrective branch choice without making late identity disposable. - tis and dis remain compatible with existing influence doctrine while now exposing spend commitments and ledger history explicitly. ### negative - evolution canon and existing docs must explicitly carry the new exception. - ledger separation creates more ui and validation complexity than a single-currency design. - death loss plus mcc repair debt create another pp governance edge case that must be explained clearly in the ui. ## related decisions - status: proposed - date: 2026-05-14 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the player system already has adaptive missions, event logs, tutorials, mcc guidance, and preference learning, but it does not yet define how the system should infer deeper character, distinguish mask from nature, or tempt players toward better conduct without removing darker paths. the game needs to support: - heroes, villains, rough protectors, counterfeit heroes, counterfeit villains, and redemption arcs - explicit player freedom to rule cruelly, govern mercifully, or oscillate between those poles - stronger-than-real-life encouragement toward courtesy, restitution, mercy, and principled behavior - a discoverable hidden system that is not displayed as a default in-game meter ## decision 1. add the quiet measure as a hidden player system sublayer for character inference rather than a visible alignment or morality bar. 2. model the hidden measure over six core axes: selflessness, give, mercy, duty, principle, and courtesy. 3. derive higher-order reads such as nature, mask, veil gap, and caste naming from those axes and their evidence windows. 4. let the quiet measure shape internal mission generation, system tone, and later judgment access. 5. bias world surplus toward virtue, courtesy, mercy, and restitution more than the real world usually does, while still allowing vice, domination, and counterfeit virtue to remain viable. 6. keep tyrant, villain, fraud, and rough-hero paths playable and consequential instead of treating them as failure states. 7. restrict default disclosure: no hud meter, no default status pane, no points-ledger representation, and no ordinary npc omniscience from raw hidden scores. 8. permit explicit judgment only when the player asks and the system has sufficient repeated evidence. 9. gate runtime activation behind the feature flag isekai.player-system.quiet-measure.enabled. ## alternatives considered - visible morality or alignment meter: - easier to explain, but too gameable and too flattening for false heroes, false villains, and redemption arcs. - purely neutral behavior model with no virtue bias: - preserves symmetry, but fails the design goal of quietly making better conduct more fertile than reality usually does. - hard-force virtue and suppress villain paths: - simpler ethically, but collapses player freedom and weakens world drama. - leave adaptive missions preference-only without hidden moral inference: - adequate for build guidance, but too weak for caste naming, judgment, and deeper social texture. ## consequences ### positive - the system can tempt players toward better habits without removing player authorship. - mission content can test who the player wants to become rather than only what build they prefer. - courtesy and restitution gain repeated mechanical relevance, which better supports real-habit transfer. - villainous or tyrannical play remains valid, but becomes more brittle, lonely, and revolt-prone in a world-consistent way. ### negative - behavioral inference, mission branching, and disclosure thresholds need careful tuning. - designers must prevent politeness from overpowering deeper signals such as mercy and reciprocity. - public package discovery and hidden in-game presentation need a stricter boundary than many ordinary feature systems. ## related decisions - tdr-0029 mission system adaptive guidance and reward governance - tdr-0031 event log and achievement projection from a blob-backed observed-event lake - tdr-0035 quiet measure hidden judgment and mission pressure - adr 0059 player system guidance layer and world-state boundary - adr 0061 mission system uses an adaptive player model with bounded rewards - adr 0063 blob-backed observed events serve player recall, achievement projection, and gossip sourcing

- validate the requested world target before runtime bootstrap begins; - make spawn versus resume selection explicit; - and emit one stable bootstrap payload that player system and renderer consumers can use without reaching back into account/profile state. the parent rollout control is the remotely managed feature flag isekai.world-entry.enabled, with break-glass env override worldentryenabled. ## decision - implement the first slice in plasius-ltd-site backend routes under post /api/player-system/world-entry. - keep the route authenticated and fail closed with 404 worldentrydisabled when the parent rollout is off. - require the world-entry bridge to consume the existing character-lifecycle contract rather than re-reading profile/account state directly. - persist resumable bootstrap sessions in a dedicated backend table worldentrysessionentity, partitioned by the authenticated account user id and keyed by worldid + activecharacterid. - model transition intent explicitly: - spawn always issues a fresh bootstrap session; status: proposed - date: 2026-05-15 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context feature #710 requires explicit timeout, idempotency, latency, and saturation controls for the service-to-game bridge that connects account-owned surfaces to authoritative gameplay systems. the current plasius-ltd-site repository does not yet host the future character-selection, world-entry, resume, party, or ai-mediation authority services named by the feature. what it does host today is the public get /api/player-system/runtime boundary used by the player system shell. if this repo pretends those future backends already exist, it would fabricate fake apis and blur the authority boundaries that adr 0059 and tdr 0027 are trying to protect. the boundary decision therefore needs to make the nfr contract explicit on the runtime surface that exists now, while leaving the later authority services responsible for their own implementation details. ## decision 1. publish a public-safe servicebridge reliability contract on get /api/player-system/runtime. 2. gate the contract behind the feature flag isekai.service-bridge.reliability.enabled, with isekaiservicebridgereliabilityenabled reserved as a break-glass-only backend override. 3. define explicit timeout budgets and p95 latency targets for the current bridge lanes: - character selection - world entry - resume hydration - party projection - ai mediation 4. require caller-owned retries and caller-supplied idempotency keys for all mutation-style bridge lanes. the runtime contract publishes the canonical header name and required lanes instead of allowing each future service to invent a different replay contract. 5. standardize the bounded degraded responses on the public contract: - 504 servicebridgetimeout - 429 servicebridgesaturated - 503 servicebridgeunavailable 6. publish the canonical observability signal names that downstream authority services must emit once they exist, and validate those names in repo policy artifacts so the contract cannot drift silently. 7. keep the runtime contract public-safe. it must not reveal storage topology, queue depths, targeted cohorts, private dependency names, credentials, or other operator-only implementation details. ## alternatives considered - implement speculative gameplay bridge apis in this repo now: - rejected because the authority services do not exist here today and fabricating them would create false confidence and poor ownership seams. - leave the nfr rules only in issue comments: - rejected because that would not give callers a runtime contract, code coverage, or machine-validated drift detection. - expose raw operational telemetry or private topology through the runtime: - rejected because the player system runtime is a public-safe contract and must not leak operator-only details. ## consequences ### positive - the service-bridge nfr contract becomes explicit, reversible, and testable on a real repo-owned boundary today. - future authority services inherit one timeout, idempotency, and degraded-mode vocabulary instead of inventing incompatible variants. - player system clients can reason about fail-closed behavior and retry ownership without guessing. ### negative - the runtime publishes policy rather than live downstream implementation telemetry, so later authority services still need to emit and alert on the documented signal names. - future repos must honor this contract rather than redefining their own timeout or replay behavior ad hoc. ## related decisions - status: proposed - date: 2026-05-16 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context feature #716 requires the site-owned service-to-game bridge surfaces to stay accessible for consumers while also keeping authority handoff seams explicit and portable across environments. the plasius-ltd-site repository still does not host the future world-entry, party-authority, or ai-mediation backends that will ultimately own those bridge lanes. what it does host today is the public get /api/player-system/runtime surface and the /player-system shell that consumes it. if this repository hard-codes localhost assumptions, aca hostnames, or direct knowledge of future service topology, it would collapse the authority boundaries protected by adr 0059 and tdr 0027. the decision therefore needs to publish a public-safe contract for bridge accessibility and seam portability on the runtime surface that already exists, while leaving later authority services responsible for their own implementation details. ## decision 1. publish a public-safe servicebridgeaccessibility contract on get /api/player-system/runtime. 2. gate the contract behind the feature flag isekai.service-bridge.accessibility-portability.enabled, with isekaiservicebridgeaccessibilityportabilityenabled reserved as a break-glass-only backend override. 3. define symbolic accessibility rules for the current site-owned bridge-fed surfaces: - identity-card projection - party-presence projection - runtime-readiness status 4. standardize the symbolic fallback channels exposed by the runtime contract: - text-and-touch for voice-unavailable flows - live-region-and-structured-summary for non-visual consumption - text-summary-and-focusable-actions for non-audio or projection-light consumption 5. publish symbolic authority seam metadata for: - world entry - party presence - ai mediation 6. keep the runtime contract public-safe. it must not reveal private topology, environment-specific hostnames, credentials, targeted flag cohorts, or any other operator-only configuration detail. 7. keep user-visible copy in frontend translations. the runtime contract publishes symbolic identifiers, while the site-local consumer maps them to translated text and accessible semantics. ## alternatives considered - hard-code environment assumptions in the frontend: - rejected because that would make localhost, aca, or future runtime choices part of the consumer contract. - expose english explanatory strings directly from the backend: - rejected because user-visible copy should remain translation-owned and symbolic contracts are easier to validate for drift. - leave seam and accessibility rules only in issue comments: - rejected because callers would have no runtime-visible contract, no code coverage, and no machine-validated policy evidence. ## consequences ### positive - the player system shell can document accessible bridge-consumer expectations without pretending to own future gameplay authorities. - authority seams become explicit and environment-safe instead of relying on undocumented deployment assumptions. - the contract remains reversible and testable behind a dedicated feature flag. ### negative - the runtime publishes symbolic policy rather than live downstream state, so future authority services still need to honor and implement the contract. - the frontend now owns the translation mapping for the published symbolic identifiers, which adds one more drift surface that policy validation must cover. ## related decisions - adr 0059: player system guidance layer and world-state boundary - adr 0068: player system runtime publishes the service-bridge reliability contract - tdr-0027 player system runtime orchestration

status: proposed - date: 2026-05-16 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context feature #712 and repo task #713 require the site-owned player system shell to publish explicit render-budget, keyboard, focus, and voice-fallback expectations. the plasius-ltd-site repository does not host the future authoritative gameplay runtime, but it does host the public get /api/player-system/runtime surface and the /player-system route that demonstrates the shell behavior. if those nfr expectations remain only in issue comments or ad hoc frontend copy, the rollout cannot be validated mechanically and consumers cannot inspect whether the guidance shell is in its baseline or rollback state. the runtime therefore needs a public-safe contract that exposes symbolic nfr expectations without leaking private topology or operator-only telemetry. ## decision 1. publish a public-safe guidancenfr contract on get /api/player-system/runtime. 2. gate the contract behind the feature flag isekai.player-system.guidance-nfr.enabled, with isekaiplayersystemguidancenfrenabled reserved as a break-glass-only backend override. 3. publish explicit p95 shell budgets for: - initial shell launch - focused module transitions - live alert/status presentation - combat-safe pane reduction 4. publish symbolic keyboard and focus expectations for: - invocation and modality toggles - module switcher controls - combat-safe active-pane continuity - live-region status updates 5. publish symbolic voice and narration fallbacks for: - voice playback unavailable - narration unavailable - speech capture unavailable 6. keep the contract public-safe. it must not expose private tracing ids, topology, targeted flag cohorts, or internal-only telemetry names. 7. keep user-visible wording in frontend translations. the runtime publishes symbolic identifiers and numeric targets, while the site consumer maps them to accessible copy. ## alternatives considered - document the shell nfrs only in readme or task comments: - rejected because there would be no runtime-visible contract and no machine-checked drift detection. - expose english prose from the backend: - rejected because translation-owned copy belongs in the frontend and the symbolic contract is easier to validate. - use frontend-only env flags for the guidance surface: - rejected because feature rollout and rollback must remain remotely controllable. ## consequences ### positive - operators and reviewers can inspect the guidance-shell nfr posture through the existing public runtime surface. - the /player-system route can show keyboard, focus, and fallback behavior in an accessible way without inventing site-local hidden assumptions. - the contract is testable and reversible under a dedicated feature flag. ### negative - the runtime publishes policy expectations rather than live measured production telemetry, so downstream observability still needs to enforce the actual service budgets separately. - the frontend now owns another symbolic-to-copy mapping surface that must stay aligned with the machine-readable policy. ## related decisions - adr 0059: player system guidance layer and world-state boundary - status accepted ## context the site now carries player system rollout documentation for core shell state, bridge reliability, shell nfr guidance, and service-bridge accessibility. what remains missing is the first bounded contract for ai-generated gameplay output. approved ai surfaces may suggest npc dialogue, npc actions, or gm-flavoured world interventions, but the runtime still needs an explicit seam that: 1. rejects raw or unapproved chatbot output as direct authority, 2. classifies accepted output into bounded mediation classes, and 3. emits stable authority-request envelopes and audit fields instead of prompt text. without that seam, a future gameplay client could accidentally treat generic ai copy as executable world authority. ## decision 1. add the parent feature flag isekai.ai-authority-bridge.enabled with isekaiaiauthoritybridgeenabled reserved as a break-glass override. 2. publish the public-safe aiauthoritybridge runtime contract on get /api/player-system/runtime so the /player-system shell can document approved sources, mediation classes, request kinds, and audit envelope fields. 3. add post /api/player-system/ai-authority-bridge as the first bounded site endpoint that accepts approved ai gameplay submissions. 4. restrict accepted source classes to: - npc-dialogue - npc-action - gm-world 5. translate accepted submissions into one of three mediation classes: - advisory - deterministic-check - operator-gated 6. return digest-backed authority-request envelopes instead of raw ai output so downstream authorities receive bounded, stable request kinds: - npc-dialogue-hint - npc-action-check - world-intervention-review 7. keep authoritative runtime and human review as the final owner of any state mutation. the bridge classifies and prepares requests; it does not mutate world state directly. ## consequences ### positive - generic chatbot output cannot silently become authoritative gameplay state. - the first ai bridge contract is reversible through a feature flag and can fail closed by default. - auditability is explicit because the bridge returns required envelope fields such as authenticated user id, correlation id, source class, classification, authority request kind, and content digest. - frontend and backend tests can pin the public contract without depending on a future private gameplay authority implementation. ### negative - the first slice documents and classifies bounded requests but does not yet connect to a full downstream world-authority service. - clients must submit approved structured payloads rather than arbitrary free text if they want deterministic or operator-gated handling. ## rejected alternatives ### let the chatbot route emit direct gameplay mutations rejected because it would collapse advisory generation and authoritative state ownership into one surface and violate the feature acceptance criteria. ### hide the contract in private backend-only docs rejected because the /player-system consumer and public runtime contract need to stay explicit, testable, and rollback-visible to meet the repo governance rules for feature flags and nfr evidence. ## status: proposed - date: 2026-05-27 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the isekai and wider plasius game initiatives need a reusable audio runtime that can play tts, diegetic sound effects, music, ambience, and system sounds. existing packages cover tts routing and cache policy (@plasius/ai-speech), voice recognition (@plasius/voice), world and scene contracts, renderer concerns, and player system presentation. they do not provide a shared playback graph, bus policy, web audio adapter, or acoustic obstruction model. placing all audio behavior inside the renderer or player system would couple playback policy to one presentation host and make non-browser or test runtimes difficult. placing tts playback in @plasius/ai-speech would mix provider orchestration with real-time audio lifecycle concerns. ## decision 1. create a dedicated package suite for game audio: - @plasius/game-audio - @plasius/game-audio-spatial - @plasius/game-audio-web - @plasius/game-audio-react 2. keep @plasius/game-audio engine-agnostic. it owns public contracts for audio commands, bus names, categories, playback policy, asset references, feature flags, preferences, telemetry events, and runtime ports. 3. keep acoustic obstruction and occlusion estimation in @plasius/game-audio-spatial. it consumes listener, emitter, obstacle, material, and optional ray/path samples through adapter ports instead of depending directly on renderer internals. 4. keep browser playback implementation in @plasius/game-audio-web. it owns web audio lifecycle, decoding, scheduling, bus graph construction, streaming playback, and application of spatial parameters. 5. keep react hooks and player system integration in @plasius/game-audio-react. it should bridge host state into audio commands without becoming the source of game-world truth. 6. reuse @plasius/ai-speech for tts route planning and cache references. playback packages accept playable references and metadata, never provider secrets. 7. use remotely controllable feature flags for rollout: - game.audio.foundation.enabled - game.audio.tts-playback.enabled - game.audio.sfx-occlusion.enabled - game.audio.music.enabled - game.audio.system-sounds.enabled - game.audio.react-provider.enabled 8. add capabilities only for user-visible audio settings, diagnostics, or entitlement surfaces, initially game.audio.controls and game.audio.diagnostics when those surfaces exist. ## alternatives considered - put playback in @plasius/renderer: - simpler for the first web scene, but it couples audio to one rendering host and makes non-renderer consumers harder. - extend @plasius/ai-speech into playback: - convenient for tts, but it conflates provider routing/cache policy with game runtime mixing, music, and world sound effects. - use a single large @plasius/audio package: - simpler package count, but it forces react, browser, and spatial concerns into one release boundary. - adopt a full third-party sound engine as the public contract: - quicker in the short term, but the plasius api would inherit an external engine's concepts and limit native or server-test portability. ## consequences ### positive - runtime contracts stay portable across browser, native, tests, and future worker-backed audio paths. - tts, music, effects, and system sounds share one policy and bus model. - acoustic occlusion can evolve independently from browser playback internals. - the player system can present audio feedback without owning the global audio graph. - package-level tasks can be assigned and validated independently. ### negative - four packages add repository and release overhead. - cross-package compatibility must be tested explicitly. - runtime hosts must wire feature flags, asset resolvers, world adapters, and user preferences before playback is useful. - acoustic occlusion starts as an approximation and needs tuning against scene/game feel. ## related decisions - adr 0053: package strategy - adr 0059: player system guidance layer and world-state boundary - adr 0063: blob-backed observed events serve player recall, achievement projection, and gossip sourcing - tdr-0036: in-game audio runtime pipeline

deploy failures in azure cli bootstrap become bounded and diagnosable; stale runner-local azure cli state is isolated behind a fresh config dir a... references github actions environments: https://docs.github.com/actions/deployment/targeting-different-environments/using-environments-for-deployment azure cli install docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli-linux for the production cd workflow on self-hosted deploy runners: # adr 0079: bounded self-hosted azure cli bootstrap for production cd ## status - accepted - date: 2026-05-27 - version: 1.0 ## tags devops, deployment, github-actions, reliability, operations ## context production releases for plasius-ltd-site must be verified through .github/workflows/cd.yml on main. the workflow already routes deploys through self-hosted runners so production release verification does not depend on hosted-runner billing or capacity. the recurring blocker on github-runner-2 was narrower: the runner already had az on path, but az version could hang before azure login started. because the old bootstrap step trusted any existing az binary and used the runner's long-lived default /.azure state, a stale or unhealthy local cli install could stall the whole release path without failing fast or self-repairing. ## decision for the production cd workflow on self-hosted deploy runners: - keep the existing self-hosted deploy path and runner selection; - create a fresh per-run azureconfigdir before any cli health check or azure login step; - enable non-interactive azure cli extension install behavior for that isolated config dir; - bound the az version health check with timeout --preserve-status; - when an az binary already exists but fails or hangs under the bounded check, attempt an in-place repair/reinstall before aborting the deploy; - preserve the existing github actions production environment, main branch gate, oidc requirement, and azure secret-sync/deploy path. ## alternatives considered - trust any existing az binary on the runner: - rejected because a present-but-hung cli is exactly the observed failure mode. - move production cd onto github-hosted runners: - rejected because hosted-runner billing/capacity is not guaranteed for this repository and the repo already has a valid self-hosted deployment path. - repair the self-hosted runner only out-of-band: - rejected because the workflow still needs a bounded, reproducible way to detect and recover from runner-local azure cli drift. ## consequences - positive: - production releases stay on the approved self-hosted path without depending on hosted-runner billing; - deploy failures in azure cli bootstrap become bounded and diagnosable; - stale runner-local azure cli state is isolated behind a fresh config dir and can self-repair before the workflow gives up. - negative: - production deploys still depend on self-hosted runner availability overall; - the workflow now owns more azure cli bootstrap logic and repair behavior. ## references - github actions environments: https://docs.github.com/actions/deployment/targeting-different-environments/using-environments-for-deployment - azure cli install docs: https://learn.microsoft.com/cli/azure/install-azure-cli-linux

status: accepted - date: 2026-05-20 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context feature #606 introduces party membership truth, allied presence, and friendly-tracking state for cooperative runtime surfaces. the roadmap adr/tdr already establish that party truth is a sibling authority to the player system, not a local overlay inference or an internal child subsystem. the site already exposes a public get /api/player-system/runtime surface for runtime/ui consumers to discover rollout-gated contract sections. the first implementation slice needs to add party truth without: - collapsing party authority into player system ownership, - leaking user/account identifiers or rollout-targeting metadata, - or requiring frontend consumers to synthesize party state from local overlay heuristics. ## decision 1. publish party truth through a dedicated runtime contract section: - get /api/player-system/runtime now includes partypresence, - the section declares authorityowner: "party-presence" and authoritymode: "service-owned-truth", - runtime consumers must treat this as upstream truth rather than deriving party state locally. 2. keep rollout control separate from player system core: - feature #606 uses isekai.party-presence.enabled, - playersystempartypresenceenabled is the break-glass/local override, - the normal production control plane remains the stored featureflagentity. 3. keep the contract character-scoped and combat-safe: - the payload exposes partyid, characterid, ally presence/separation, friendly-tracking summaries, and shared-objective identifiers, - the payload does not expose user ids, account ids, targeted-user rollout metadata, or credential-bearing state. 4. reuse the existing player system runtime route as the public delivery shell: - the route remains an aggregator for public-safe runtime sections, - ownership stays explicit inside each section so sibling services are not mistaken for player system-owned truth. ## consequences ### positive - runtime overlays gain one explicit backend source for party membership and allied presence. - cooperative routing identifiers become stable for downstream consumers. - privacy boundaries stay narrower because the contract is character-scoped. - rollout remains independently reversible from player system core behavior. ### negative - player-system/runtime now aggregates another sibling authority section, so runtime consumers must respect per-section ownership metadata instead of assuming one uniform authority. - the first slice is static contract data until a later authoritative presence source is wired behind the same section. ## related decisions - adr 0059: player system guidance layer and world-state boundary - adr 0060: identity system uses projected status overlays over line-of-sight targets - road-map adr 0006: party presence and friendly-tracking truth require a dedicated service boundary

adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0081-moderation-escalation-review-workflow.md moderation escalation review behind a dedicated rollout flag accepted 2026-05-20 context decision related decisions context the moderation review workspace added in adr 0032 lets moderators inspect evidence and record findings, but story #490 also requires an escalation path for permanent suspension recommendations. that path introduces separate operational risks: decision 1. keep route access capability-driven: admin.route.moderation still governs whether the user may reach /admin/moderation. 2. gate recommendation routing with a second server-side feature flag: admin.moderation.escalation.enabled controls creation of perman... related decisions adr 0032: moderation evidence review behind a server-side rollout flag adr 0033: linked-identity security events in the shared audit and notification plane 1. keep route access capability-driven: admin.route.moderation still governs whether the user may reach /admin/moderation. 2. gate recommendation routing with a second server-side feature flag: admin.moderation.escalation.enabled controls creation of perman... # adr 0081: moderation escalation review behind a dedicated rollout flag - status: accepted - date: 2026-05-20 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the moderation review workspace added in adr 0032 lets moderators inspect evidence and record findings, but story #490 also requires an escalation path for permanent suspension recommendations. that path introduces separate operational risks: - moderators need to notify internal reviewers when a high-risk recommendation is created, - recommendation creation must fail closed when reviewer routing is not configured, - the escalation workflow should be reversible without removing the broader moderation evidence-review route, - later approval handlers must preserve separation of duties between the recommender and the final approver. ## decision 1. keep route access capability-driven: - admin.route.moderation still governs whether the user may reach /admin/moderation. 2. gate recommendation routing with a second server-side feature flag: - admin.moderation.escalation.enabled controls creation of permanent suspension recommendations, - the backend workspace exposes the resolved flag state to the frontend so the ui does not duplicate rollout logic in local env flags. 3. keep recommendation records site-local: - recommendation entities and workspace payloads remain inside plasius-ltd-site, - no new public package is introduced until another runtime actually needs the same moderation escalation contract. 4. treat reviewer notification configuration as required: - recommendation creation fails with a bounded configuration error when adminmoderationrevieweremails is empty, - reviewer notifications are queued through the existing notification outbox so delivery keeps the current retry/dead-letter semantics. 5. require structured evidence on recommendation submission: - moderators must provide an evidence rationale and cite at least two transcript segments from the selected case before a recommendation can be queued, - recommendation records persist those evidence citations so later approvers can review the exact transcript excerpts that triggered escalation. 6. compute recommendation-threshold heuristics on the backend: - critical incidents may escalate directly when evidence is sufficient, - non-critical incidents must satisfy a repeat-offender threshold derived from multiple high-risk cases for the same reported account, - the workspace exposes the resolved heuristic guidance to the frontend so the operator sees the threshold outcome before submission. 7. enforce separation of duties at final approval: - recommendation records explicitly require independent approval, - only service-admin or admin reviewers may approve final suspension, - the approval route rejects attempts where the recommender also acts as the final approver, - approved records retain approver identity, approval summary, and approval timestamp for later audit review. ## consequences ### positive - the escalation workflow can be disabled independently from the evidence-review workspace. - reviewer visibility becomes a hard requirement rather than a best-effort side effect. - recommendation payloads become evidence-bearing contracts instead of free-text escalation notes. - notification delivery reuses the existing outbox retries and dead-letter behavior. - final suspension approval now has an explicit independent-review boundary instead of relying on later policy interpretation. ### negative - moderation now depends on a second rollout control and reviewer-recipient configuration. - moderators must now assemble explicit evidence citations before the escalation path can proceed. - recommendation contracts remain site-local until a broader shared need is proven. - moderation approvers now need service-admin or admin authority in addition to the route capability that exposes /admin/moderation. ## related decisions - adr 0032: moderation evidence review behind a server-side rollout flag - adr 0033: linked-identity security events in the shared audit and notification plane

adrs.searchText: plasius-ltd-site plasius-ltd/plasius-ltd-site docs/adrs/adr-0082-moderation-temporary-ban-lifecycle-behind-rollout-flag.md moderation temporary-ban lifecycle behind a dedicated rollout flag accepted 2026-05-21 context decision related decisions context story #489 extends the existing moderation evidence-review workspace with a new enforcement path for temporary account bans. the moderation route already exists and adr 0032 already defines how the evidence-review workspace rolls out, but the new enforcemen... decision 1. keep moderation-route access capability-led and add a second rollout gate for the temporary-ban lifecycle: admin.route.moderation still controls whether a signed-in admin session can reach /admin/moderation, admin.moderation.temporary-ban.enabled control... related decisions adr 0025: user-scoped capabilities as the single control surface (with target routing) adr 0032: moderation evidence review behind a server-side rollout flag adr 0033: linked-identity security events in the shared audit and notification plane adr 0039: acco... 1. keep moderation-route access capability-led and add a second rollout gate for the temporary-ban lifecycle: admin.route.moderation still controls whether a signed-in admin session can reach /admin/moderation, admin.moderation.temporary-ban.enabled control... # adr 0082: moderation temporary-ban lifecycle behind a dedicated rollout flag - status: accepted - date: 2026-05-21 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context story #489 extends the existing moderation evidence-review workspace with a new enforcement path for temporary account bans. the moderation route already exists and adr 0032 already defines how the evidence-review workspace rolls out, but the new enforcement behavior adds separate operational and account-lifecycle requirements: - moderators need an auditable, reversible way to apply a time-bounded account restriction to the reported account from the evidence-review workspace, - authentication and refresh-token rotation must deny access while the ban is active, - the system must keep deterministic expiry behavior even if the rollout for new bans is later paused, - user notification, audit evidence, and moderator confirmation must all be consistent with the existing admin-control-plane safety rules, - the workflow must rate-limit moderator churn so repeated apply or update actions do not create noisy audit, session, and notification storms. this work also carries explicit nfr requirements around privacy-safe audit events, bounded failure handling, input validation, reversible rollout, and operator-visible rollback behavior. ## decision 1. keep moderation-route access capability-led and add a second rollout gate for the temporary-ban lifecycle: - admin.route.moderation still controls whether a signed-in admin session can reach /admin/moderation, - admin.moderation.temporary-ban.enabled controls whether moderators may create or update temporary bans, - adminmoderationtemporarybanenabled is reserved as the break-glass or local-development override. 2. make the owned account record the source of truth for temporary-ban state: - accountsentity stores the active case reference, reason, policy reference, apply metadata, expiry timestamp, cooldown timestamp, and last lifecycle action, - temporary-ban enforcement is evaluated through the existing owned-account access gate so login, callback, and refresh-token flows block consistently. 3. keep destructive mutation safety on the existing admin confirmation plane: - apply, update, and revoke actions require the existing destructive confirmation token plus typed intent confirmation, - all invalid, denied, successful, revoked, and expired transitions write to the shared audit plane under admin.moderation.temporary-ban. 4. separate rollout rollback from active-ban cleanup: - disabling admin.moderation.temporary-ban.enabled stops new apply or update actions, - already active bans remain enforceable until explicit revoke or scheduled expiry, - revoke stays available for active bans even while the rollout is disabled, so operators can unwind mistakes without re-enabling the rollout. 5. use deterministic expiry and bounded moderator cooldowns: - expiry is processed by a timer-driven backend worker on adminmoderationtemporarybanexpiryschedule, - expiry clears the stored ban state and records an audit event, - repeated apply or update actions enter a 10-minute cooldown window to reduce accidental churn and repeated notifications, - duration is validated to a bounded 1-168 hour window. 6. keep the moderation temporary-ban contract site-local for now: - the admin route payloads, workspace projections, and lifecycle helpers stay inside plasius-ltd-site, - no new public @plasius/ package is introduced until a second runtime needs the same moderation enforcement model. ## consequences ### positive - moderators can apply time-bounded enforcement without inventing a permanent suspension path. - account access enforcement is centralized in the existing owned-account lifecycle checks, which keeps auth behavior consistent across session flows. - rollout remains reversible for new mutations while active bans still expire deterministically. - audit and notification evidence stay on the existing shared control planes rather than adding a second moderation-specific mechanism. - cooldown and confirmation controls reduce accidental repeated moderator actions. ### negative - the site now owns another lifecycle helper, timer worker, and rollout evaluator. - /admin/moderation can stay visible while the temporary-ban action is disabled, so the workspace must explain that managed-disabled state clearly. - rollback of an already-applied ban requires an explicit revoke or waiting for expiry; disabling the rollout flag alone does not restore access. - the temporary-ban contract is still site-local and may need later extraction if other runtimes adopt the same enforcement model. ## related decisions - adr 0025: user-scoped capabilities as the single control surface (with target routing) - adr 0032: moderation evidence review behind a server-side rollout flag - adr 0033: linked-identity security events in the shared audit and notification plane - adr 0039: account soft-delete lifecycle behind a dedicated rollout flag

status: proposed - date: 2026-06-04 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context plasius now has dedicated repositories for @plasius/asset-contracts, @plasius/asset-pipeline, @plasius/asset-processing, @plasius/asset-review, and @plasius/asset-mcp. those package boundaries were scaffolded before plasius-ltd-site recorded the site-level decision that explains why the asset lifecycle is split this way, which rollout controls govern it, and how local-import seed assets relate to future ai-generated assets. without a canonical site adr: - package repos can drift on state names or responsibilities; - mcp actions can risk becoming a bypass around approval and promotion rules; - local-import flows can diverge from ai-generated flows even though they should share one governed lifecycle; - operator guidance for rollout, approval, and rollback remains implicit. ## decision 1. use one dedicated package family for the unified ai asset pipeline: - @plasius/asset-contracts - @plasius/asset-pipeline - @plasius/asset-processing - @plasius/asset-review - @plasius/asset-mcp 2. keep all asset sources on one governed lifecycle, including: - local-import - ai-generate - ai-modify - texture-regenerate - processor-retry 3. treat @plasius/asset-contracts as the canonical public vocabulary for asset identity, manifests, screenshot plans, review reports, and promotion metadata. 4. keep orchestration and state-transition policy in @plasius/asset-pipeline instead of mixing it into processing or mcp tool packages. 5. keep processing contracts in @plasius/asset-processing, review policy in @plasius/asset-review, and bounded tool or request surfaces in @plasius/asset-mcp. 6. gate the lifecycle behind the parent feature flag asset.pipeline.unified-ai-assets.enabled. 7. gate operator-visible mutation surfaces with capabilities: - asset.pipeline.mcp.manage - asset.pipeline.review.approve 8. require manifest-backed approval before promotion and explicit rollback records after any demotion or reversal. 9. use the eames lounge chair and ottoman validation asset as the first documented local-import seed so the lifecycle is grounded in a real example. ## alternatives considered - keep asset lifecycle logic inside plasius-ltd-site only: - rejected because contracts, processing, review, and mcp actions must be reusable across backend, ci, tooling, and future runtime consumers. - collapse the lifecycle into one @plasius/asset-pipeline package: - rejected because it couples public contracts, orchestration, processing, review, and mcp boundaries into one release unit. - split ai-generated and local-import assets into different pipelines: - rejected because review, approval, manifesting, promotion, and rollback must follow one policy model regardless of how the asset entered the system. - let mcp tooling promote assets directly: - rejected because mcp must remain a bounded control surface rather than a bypass around approval capability checks and immutable promotion records. ## consequences ### positive - package ownership is explicit and auditable. - local-import seed assets and ai-generated assets follow one lifecycle. - rollout and operator access controls are documented before broader implementation work. - package repos can evolve independently while sharing one site-level contract. ### negative - five packages create more release and compatibility management overhead. - follow-on tasks must keep package readme references aligned with the canonical site docs. - the lifecycle still needs implementation work in service, review, and runtime layers before promotion is end-to-end. ## related documents - docs/design/unified-ai-asset-pipeline.md - docs/tdrs/tdr-0004-unified-ai-asset-pipeline.md

status: accepted - date: 2026-06-05 - updated: 2026-06-27 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the /gpu-demo product studio mode originally pointed at a local vite-only /data/models/eames-lounge-chair-ottoman/... path. in production that path can fall through to the spa document, causing the gltf loader to parse html as json. the azure storage account used by the site has public blob access disabled, so the site cannot rely on anonymous raw blob storage urls for product studio model assets. ## decision 1. store product studio model assets in a private gpu-demo-assets blob container managed by the production cd workflow. 2. expose first-party asset urls through get /api/gpu-demo/assets/{assetpath}. 3. return the product studio model url through get /api/gpu-demo/runtime as productstudioassets.modelurl. 4. return a bounded product studio model catalog through productstudioassets.models[], sourced from deployment-assets/gpu-demo/product-studio/manifest.json, while keeping productstudioassets.modelurl as a backward-compatible pointer to the default catalog model. 5. keep the frontend from hardcoding local /data paths for production product studio mode. 6. restrict the anonymous asset route to the bounded gpu demo asset prefix, manifest-declared model ids, and known static asset extensions. ## consequences - the frontend no longer ships the eames bundle through frontend/public. - the gltf loader receives a stable first-party model url, and relative buffer references resolve through the same backend route. - the frontend can support additional product studio models by selecting from runtime catalog entries instead of shipping one-off route code for each model. - the backend remains the boundary that protects private blob storage from direct public access or credential leakage. - cd must seed the gpu-demo-assets container before production validation. ## alternatives considered - public blob storage container: - rejected because account-level public blob access is disabled. - sas urls in runtime payloads: - rejected because public runtime metadata should not expose secret-bearing query strings. - frontend public/ assets: - rejected because the product studio asset source should be blob-backed and controlled by backend runtime metadata. ## related decisions - self-hosted deploy failures fail fast and with clearer diagnostics; hosted fallback remains available when no azure-ready self-hosted runner i... references adr 0079: bounded self-hosted azure cli bootstrap for production cd github self-hosted runner labels: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-runners/self-hosted-runners/apply-labels for plasius-ltd-site production cd: # adr 0087: explicit azure-ready runner selection for production cd ## status - accepted - date: 2026-06-11 - version: 1.0 ## tags devops, deployment, github-actions, reliability, operations ## context adr 0079 bounded the azure cli bootstrap step for self-hosted production deploys, but issue #1014 showed that generic self-hosted linux/x64 labels were still too broad for the deploy lane. the workflow could select a runner that did not actually provide a healthy azure cli, then spend several minutes attempting repair during the production deploy itself. that behavior kept the approved .github/workflows/cd.yml path intact, but it did not create a reliable contract for which runners are safe to receive production azure deploy jobs. ## decision for plasius-ltd-site production cd: - self-hosted deploy runners must advertise an explicit custom azure-cli label in addition to the default self-hosted, linux, and x64 labels; status: accepted - date: 2026-06-16 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the current site-owned voice pipeline is deliberately narrow: it exposes bounded speech-to-text and rude-word moderation routes behind voice.pipeline.production.enabled, with explicit timeout budgets and no fake fallback output. the vai responsiveness rollout adds a broader voice interaction surface where two request classes compete for the same infrastructure: - command or incantation-style utterances that must stay cheap, deterministic, and measurably fast; - conversation turns that can justify richer reasoning, memory use, and more expensive voice output. if the system treats every utterance as free-form conversation first, command latency, cost, and route predictability will drift upward and downstream features will not know where structured parsing ends and model-driven dialogue begins. ## decision 1. separate voice traffic into command and conversation lanes before any large-model reasoning step. 2. require the speech-to-text contract used by the router to emit the following fields in one pass: - transcript - confidence - utterancetypehint - openingverb - timing metadata for speech start, speech end, and total utterance length 3. classify every utterance into one of four router-owned categories: - command - conversation-opener - active-conversation-turn - invalid-or-unclear 4. keep command handling deterministic and ordered: - grammar parse first - alias and fuzzy correction second - clarification prompt third - large-model escalation only when the route remains unresolved after the deterministic path or when the user is clearly in the conversation lane 5. keep conversation handling responsible for: - dialogue planning - memory selection - response shaping - tts richness choices delegated from the degradation policy 6. keep routing and classification server-side or edge-side. the frontend may capture ui timing, but it must not become the source of truth for utterance type classification or route choice. 7. publish route telemetry that downstream implementation work must emit: - utterance category - classifier confidence band - parse resolution path - clarification count - command-lane latency measured separately from conversation first-audio 8. treat the routing boundary as rollout-sensitive work for downstream implementation. the first implementing feature must introduce a remotely controllable router flag before live traffic depends on this split. ## alternatives considered - route every utterance through one conversational model first: - rejected because it makes command handling slower, more expensive, and harder to reason about when near-miss phrasing should still resolve cheaply. - use keyword-only routing with no classifier contract: - rejected because it is too brittle for mixed command and conversational speech and cannot explain ambiguous turns cleanly. - let the browser classify command versus conversation locally: - rejected because it would duplicate policy, leak routing drift across clients, and weaken auditability. ## consequences ### positive - downstream features inherit one clear ownership boundary between stt, classification, parsing, routing, and conversation work. - command latency can be measured independently against the <=500 ms p50 objective already named for the fast path. - test plans can target command parsing and clarification without involving conversation-model behavior. ### negative - the stt contract becomes richer and therefore needs contract coverage across local-first and cloud-backed implementations. - ambiguous utterances must surface clarification behavior intentionally instead of silently flowing into free-form conversation. ## related decisions - adr 0053: package strategy - adr 0072: player system runtime publishes the service-bridge reliability contract - adr 0076: in-game audio package boundaries and acoustic occlusion - docs/how-to-guides/voice-pipeline-rollout-controls.md

status: accepted - date: 2026-06-16 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the vai roadmap needs a policy that makes most low-value or high-volume voice interactions cheaper and faster before the system hard-refuses work. a single "healthy versus degraded" switch is not enough because route choice depends on more than platform health: - remaining budget - user or npc patience - rude or abusive interaction state - current latency pressure - cache confidence - model availability without one explicit degradation contract, later routing, cache, telemetry, and runbook work will encode incompatible ideas of how the voice system should get shorter, cheaper, less rich, or less willing under pressure. ## decision 1. route selection must combine cache probability, budget state, rudeness state, npc importance, patience class, live load, latency class, and model availability instead of depending on any single cost or health variable. 2. weighted model selection is the default policy inside each response stage: - cheaper and faster local or small-model paths should win when they satisfy the current stage requirements; - premium-cloud paths are reserved for high-value or high-need cases and are treated as explicit overflow rather than the baseline route. 3. standardize degradation stages 0 through 4: - stage 0: full-fidelity behavior with richest memory, personality, and tts options allowed by the route. - stage 1: efficient default behavior with moderate response-length caps and reduced premium preference. - stage 2: bounded concise behavior with shallower memory and less personality richness. - stage 3: terse utility behavior that prioritizes clarity, safety, and latency over richness. - stage 4: clarification-only, template-only, or explicit unavailable behavior when the route cannot remain safe, fast, or affordable. 4. every degradation stage must define and enforce all of the following control dimensions: - model tier - response length - memory depth - personality richness - tts richness - willingness to continue free-form conversation 5. rudeness and abuse are first-class routing inputs. rude or hostile state may shorten replies, reduce expressive tts richness, or end conversational willingness earlier than budget-only pressure would. 6. budget policy and tone policy remain related but separate: - budget limits bound cost and premium usage; - rudeness and patience shape how willing or rich the system remains; - neither policy may silently override the other without explicit stage definitions. 7. preserve privacy in route telemetry: - emit stage, cache-hit type, model tier, budget band, and rudeness band; - do not emit raw transcript or synthesized reply text as standard telemetry. 8. keep open experimental parameters explicit rather than pretending they are already tuned: - patience decay rates - npc importance weighting - premium escape-hatch thresholds - per-stage word or token caps these parameters must be validated by the mixed-load experimentation feature before production thresholds are treated as settled. ## alternatives considered - use a binary healthy/degraded policy: - rejected because it cannot express the different ways the system should get shorter, cheaper, and less willing before total refusal. - optimize routing only for lowest cost: - rejected because cost-only routing would ignore user patience, abuse state, and route-specific latency expectations. - make moderation or rude-word handling a separate post-processing step: - rejected because tone, willingness, and tts richness must shape route choice earlier than final response formatting. ## consequences ### positive - later implementation can explain why a request used a given model tier, cache path, or response-length cap. - cost control, user patience, and abuse posture become tunable without redefining the whole routing stack. - dashboards and experiments can inspect degradation behavior stage by stage instead of collapsing everything into one failure bucket. ### negative - the policy surface is broader and requires deliberate validation before the open parameters harden into production defaults. - weighted routing must be observable enough to avoid "mystery" route changes during incidents or cost spikes. ## related decisions - adr 0053: package strategy - adr 0072: player system runtime publishes the service-bridge reliability contract - adr 0088: voice ai separates command and conversation routing before large-model work - docs/how-to-guides/voice-pipeline-rollout-controls.md

status: accepted - date: 2026-06-16 - decision makers: plasius engineering ## context the vai roadmap already names the operational outcomes that matter: - first-audio responsiveness for conversation - separate command-latency reporting - cache hit rate - premium-cloud share - reply-length drift - edge-service runbooks and failover readiness if later telemetry, dashboard, and edge-bootstrap work start without one topology and slo contract, teams will disagree about where stt and tts should run, which signals page operators, and when premium overflow is normal versus a rollout failure. ## decision 1. use an edge-first topology for the latency-sensitive front of the route: - stt streaming or fast transcription start - utterance classification - cache lookup - deterministic command parsing - local-first tts start when an approved edge voice path is healthy 2. keep the site-owned backend as the control plane for: - feature-flag evaluation - identity and session context - policy configuration - audit and operator metadata - premium overflow authorization 3. treat premium cloud inference and premium tts as overflow or high-value lanes, not the default path for routine voice turns. 4. freeze the initial responsiveness envelope and alert thresholds that later dashboard and runbook work must implement: - conversation first-audio p50 target: = 2200 ms - warning when 2200 ms - critical when > 3000 ms - conversation first-audio p90 target: = 5000 ms - warning when 5000 ms - critical when > 7000 ms - command latency p50 target: = 500 ms - warning when 500 ms - critical when > 900 ms - small-talk cache hit floor: - warning when 40% - critical when < 25% - premium-cloud share ceiling: - warning when 10% - critical when > 20% 5. make reply-length drift a mandatory dashboard signal from the start, but keep its warning and critical thresholds open until mixed-load experimentation establishes stable route-type baselines. 6. require dashboards to report at minimum: - p25, p50, and p90 latency by route type - first-audio timing - command trigger latency - cache-hit distribution by cache tier - premium-cloud share - reply-length drift - degradation-stage mix 7. require edge-service bootstrap and incident runbooks to inherit this adr's ownership split: - edge teams own health probes, concurrency ceilings, queue or saturation signals, cold-start behavior, and local-first failover posture; - site operators own control-plane flags, premium overflow policy, alert routing, and rollback coordination. 8. treat future implementation work as rollout-sensitive. the first telemetry and edge-bootstrap features must introduce remotely controllable flags before live traffic depends on these paths. ## alternatives considered -
